title: Review convenience implementations for `vctrs_vctr`
description:
Currently unclear what are the consequences of the special handling of `vctrs_vctr` classes. It makes me nervous that rcrds and list-ofs inherit from the current behaviour that I don't understand well. I think we need a better and clearer foundation for the convenience implementations.

Should `vctrs_vctr` classes inherit from the base coercion diagram, i.e. if the base type is double it's coercible to integer and logical automatically? Should this be by default or opt-in? Should this be only for classes that don't implement any `vec_ptype2()` methods?

title: Combine data frames in parallel in `vec_c()` and `vec_rbind()`
description:
* Save column pointers as in the hashing code, for the output and for all the inputs.

* Once we have only array pointers we can assign in parallel.

* List-cols involve the R API and so must be assigned separately.

* df-cols could in principle be assigned in parallel too, but this would be a bit more complex.

Should make a big improvement when recombining data frames with `vec_unchop()`.

Technical challenge: Figure out recursive proxying and restoration. Will require keeping a tree of restoration targets. Also need to think through interaction with method composition of proxy and restore.

title: Allow for unnamed data frame input in dictionary functions
description:
``` r
library(vctrs)
x <- new_data_frame(list(1, 2))
vec_unique_count(x)
#> Error in vec_unique_count(x): STRING_ELT() can only be applied to a 'character vector', not a 'NULL'
```

I don't think that an unnamed data frame is always a "corrupt" data frame.

I think that creating a data frame can be a useful signal that you want to use a row wise vctrs function, even if you don't know the column names. For example, consider this alternate `n_distinct()` implementation. The `set_names()` line is currently required and is actually pretty expensive when called a large number of times, but should not be necessary if `vec_unique_count()` didn't error here

```r
n_distinct <- function(..., na.rm = FALSE) {
  size <- vec_size_common(...)
  
  x <- vec_recycle_common(..., .size = size)
  #x <- set_names(x, seq_along(x))
  x <- new_data_frame(x, n = size)
  
  if (isTRUE(na.rm)){
    x <- vec_slice(x, !reduce(map(x, vec_equal_na), `|`))
  }
  
  vec_unique_count(x)
}
```

title: Add function to show prototype constructor
description:
In functions that guess the prototype e.g. with `vec_ptype_common` it would be great to be able to print the constructor instead of only the prototype itself. For example in the following code

``` r
df <- tidyr::tibble(x = list(list(a = 1L), list(a = 0.5)))

tidyr::hoist(
  df,
  "x",
  "a"
)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 1
#>       a
#>   <dbl>
#> 1   1  
#> 2   0.5
```

<sup>Created on 2020-07-16 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

it would be nice to help the user with useable code (e.g. like in `dplyr::left_join()`) for the `.ptype` argument, e.g. something like

```
Use
  .ptype = list(
    a = double()
  )
to be explicit about the prototypes
```

With `vec_ptype_full()` one gets a nicely printable prototype but one cannot use the text directly in code. So adding a function `vec_ptype_constructor()` would be a useful addition.

title: Improperly placed type check?
description:
There was a new type check added here
https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/671dd82c6af02a2cdc5b3b26795f521dfa199609/src/slice-assign.c#L427-L431

This breaks lubridate's vctrs methods which were working before.

I think this either isn't the right place for this, or it isn't required. The problem is that `value_elt` has not yet been proxied. That doesn't happen until later on in `vec_proxy_assign_opts()`. So in lubridate I have a `proxy_elt` that was a data frame, and a `value_elt` that was a Period object. The proxy of this `value_elt` is a data frame, but it hasn't been taken yet so this check complains.

title: vec_rbind() performance regression on R 4.0 with df-cols
description:
Performance regression when rbinding lots of data frames that have df-cols. I'm sure this has to do with making extra copies, but I'm not sure where yet. I'll take a look.

This is with dev vctrs.

R 3.6

```r
library(vctrs)

df_col <- new_data_frame(list(x = 1:2))
df <- new_data_frame(list(y = df_col))

x <- rep_len(list(df), 10000)
y <- rep_len(list(df_col), 10000)

lst_rbind <- function(x) {
  vec_rbind(!!!x)
}

bench::mark(lst_rbind(x))
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   expression        min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>   <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 lst_rbind(x)   37.5ms   37.9ms      26.2     277KB     52.4

bench::mark(lst_rbind(y))
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   expression        min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>   <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 lst_rbind(y)   16.5ms   18.2ms      55.1     274KB     16.5
```

R 4.0

```r
library(vctrs)

df_col <- new_data_frame(list(x = 1:2))
df <- new_data_frame(list(y = df_col))

x <- rep_len(list(df), 10000)
y <- rep_len(list(df_col), 10000)

lst_rbind <- function(x) {
  vec_rbind(!!!x)
}

bench::mark(lst_rbind(x))
#> Warning: Some expressions had a GC in every iteration; so filtering is disabled.
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   expression        min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>   <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 lst_rbind(x)    316ms    352ms      2.84     764MB     48.2

bench::mark(lst_rbind(y))
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   expression        min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>   <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 lst_rbind(y)   15.8ms   17.6ms      55.6     274KB     23.4
```

title: Feature Request: Add tolerance control to integer maybe_lossy_cast()
description:
When casting from double to integer, it would help to have a tolerance argument.  I often load data from sources with less-than-perfect fidelity (e.g. MS Excel files) where integers have floating point error introduced as part of the file format.  (e.g. something like 0.2 => 0.2000000002 commonly appears).

It would help if `maybe_lossy_cast()` for the `.integer` casts would accept a tolerance argument to allow something intermediate between completely permissive casting with `allow_lossy_cast()` and the loss of `loss_type="precision"`

I think that this would take the form of an argument like `tol_integer=0` where `tol_integer` would be a double between 0 (current behavior) and 1 (completely permissive, the equivalent of `allow_lossy_cast()`).

Also, `maybe_lossy_cast(... loss_type="precision")` does not appear to allow loss of precision in a double-to-integer cast (see the last line of the reprex):

``` r
library(vctrs)
vec_cast(c(NA, 1, 1.1), to=integer())
#> Error: Can't convert from <double> to <integer> due to loss of precision.
#> * Locations: 3
allow_lossy_cast(vec_cast(c(NA, 1, 1.1), to=integer()))
#> [1] NA  1  1
maybe_lossy_cast(vctrs::vec_cast(c(NA, 1, 1.1), to=integer()), loss_type="precision")
#> Error: Can't convert from <double> to <integer> due to loss of precision.
#> * Locations: 3
```

title: A paste with NA handling
description:
This might sound a bit out of scope but I think there's a place for this function somewhere. 

I'm trying to do something very simple, which is concatenate a bunch of character columns in a data frame. The go to is `tidyr::unite` but my data set has a lot of NA values. `unite` concatenates vectors with `paste`, which means the result will be full of "blah, NA, blah, ...". There's a discussion of this here tidyverse/tidyr#203. 

The simple solution is just to sub in a `paste` function that handled `NA`s and it seemed weird to me that this didn't already exist but googling just brought up more [discussion](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/13673894/suppress-nas-in-paste) with some hacky and slow pure R solutions. 

So I think there's a need for a low level `paste(..., sep = " ", collapse = NULL, na.rm = FALSE)` and maybe vctrs is that place?

title: Switch to `MAYBE_SHARED()` in `r_maybe_duplicate()`
description:
`MAYBE_REFERENCED()` returns true if there is only 1 reference. `MAYBE_SHARED()` returns false in this case.

This won't matter much for a while even when R switches to reference count because the namedness/refcount of objects is bumped to NAMEDMAX when a promise is resolved. For this reason, even temporaries won't be considered safe for mutation:

```r
# `1:100` is wrapped in a promise, evaluated by `.Call()`, and bumped to NAMEDMAX
vec_assign(1:100, 1, 10)
```

However when R solves this issue with promises, we should be able to get perf improvements with temporaries. But for this we'll need to allow 1 reference, the one held by the closure wrapper.

Switching to it right away would also make it easier to assess performance in the no-copy cases, see https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/pull/837#issuecomment-588124814.

title: "Some attributes are incompatible" error
description:
I has been notified that the {quantities} package has a broken vignette on CRAN. This is the error:

``` r
library(quantities)
#> Loading required package: units
#> udunits system database from /usr/share/udunits
#> Loading required package: errors
iris.q <- iris
for (i in 1:4)
  quantities(iris.q[,i]) <- list("cm", iris.q[,i] * 0.05)

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts=FALSE)
iris.q %>%
  group_by(Species) %>%
  summarise_all(mean)
#> Error: Problem with `summarise()` input `Sepal.Length`.
#> x Input `Sepal.Length` must return compatible vectors across groups
#> ℹ Input `Sepal.Length` is `(function (x, ...) ...`.
#> ℹ Result type for group 1 (Species = "setosa"): <quantities>.
#> ℹ Result type for group 2 (Species = "versicolor"): <quantities>.
```

How are groups with the same class incompatible? I tracked down the issue a little bit. A {quantities} object has two parts: {units} and {errors}. Just with {units}, it works ok:

```r
iris.q %>%
  mutate_at(1:4, drop_errors) %>%
  group_by(Species) %>%
  summarise_all(mean)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 5
#>   Species    Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width
#>   <fct>              [cm]        [cm]         [cm]        [cm]
#> 1 setosa            5.006       3.428        1.462       0.246
#> 2 versicolor        5.936       2.770        4.260       1.326
#> 3 virginica         6.588       2.974        5.552       2.026
```

But not with {errors}:

```r
iris.q %>%
  mutate_at(1:4, drop_units) %>%
  group_by(Species) %>%
  summarise_all(mean)
#> Error: Problem with `summarise()` input `Sepal.Length`.
#> x Input `Sepal.Length` must return compatible vectors across groups
#> ℹ Input `Sepal.Length` is `(function (x, ...) ...`.
#> ℹ Result type for group 1 (Species = "setosa"): <errors>.
#> ℹ Result type for group 2 (Species = "versicolor"): <errors>.
```

I continued tracking the issue down to `vec_ptype_common`, which works for {units}:

```r
c(set_units(1, m), set_units(3, m))
#> Units: [m]
#> [1] 1 3
vctrs::vec_ptype_common(set_units(1, m), set_units(3, m))
#>  [m]
```

but not for {errors}:

```r
c(set_errors(1, 0.1), set_errors(3, 0.2))
#> Errors: 0.1 0.2
#> [1] 1 3
vctrs::vec_ptype_common(set_errors(1, 0.1), set_errors(3, 0.2))
#> Error: Can't combine `..1` <errors> and `..2` <errors>.
#> x Some attributes are incompatible.
#> ℹ The author of the class should implement vctrs methods.
#> ℹ See <https://vctrs.r-lib.org/reference/faq-error-incompatible-attributes.html>.
```

We are going to implement glue for {vctrs}, as we discussed in https://github.com/r-quantities/units/issues/239, but shouldn't this work? And if so, it would be great if the fix makes it into the planned patch release, so that I don't have to apply a quick workaround to retain {quantities} on CRAN.

title: Fix sf combination with multiple chunks
description:
From https://github.com/r-spatial/sf/issues/1390#issuecomment-636536316

```r
sfc <- sf::st_sfc(sf::st_point())
sf <- sf::st_sf(geo = sfc)

vctrs::vec_rbind(sf, sf)
#> Simple feature collection with 2 features and 0 fields (with 2 geometries empty)
#> geometry type:  POINT
#> dimension:      XY
#> bbox:           xmin: NA ymin: NA xmax: NA ymax: NA
#> CRS:            NA
#>           geo
#> 1 POINT EMPTY
#> 2 POINT EMPTY

vctrs::vec_rbind(sf, sf, sf)
#> Error in st_geometry.sf(x) :
#>   attr(obj, "sf_column") does not point to a geometry column.
#> Did you rename it, without setting st_geometry(obj) <- "newname"?
```

This is a bad interaction between the `c()` fallback in `vec_rbind()`, which currently creates a sentinel column in the common type, and the same-type fallback for foreign data frames, which calls `[<-` to update the inputs with the common-type column structure.

title: What's the best way to use an expressions as an attribute to a vctrs object?
description:
Hi,

I've been trying to apply vctrs to some of my code. Ones with regular attributes seem to be working well now.

However, some of my objects need expressions as one of their attributes.

I'm aware we are now introducing the problem that you can't have a vector of expressions, but I'm struggling to understand how to work around that in this context (I am assuming that you can't have a vector of expressions, but you can in principle have a vector of objects for whom a parameter is an expression).

How do I define the ptype (eg for use with vec_assert) of expr? Its type is reported as a language. Both base::call() and rlang::call2() can't be called without parameters. 

I've tried using rlang::exprs() and getting the convenience type to place the expression into a list of 1. That works, but then causes problems eg within the environment browser pane, where we trigger the inevitable: `Error in FUN(X[[i]], ...) : object of type 'symbol' is not subsettable` (presumably because it's a named list).

Is there a recommended way to work with expressions in this context?

title: Helpers for data frame subclass extensions
description:
I've now added vctrs/dplyr support for rsample’s data frame subclasses, and for one of dials’s data frame subclasses. A few common pieces are emerging that get used in the dplyr and vctrs methods:

- `<subclass>_strip(x)` - Strips off all attributes related to the subclass and returns a bare tibble. It is careful to retain all attributes on `x` that are not related to the `<subclass>`

- `<subclass>_reconstruct(x, to)` - This is an inlined version of `dplyr_reconstruct.data.frame()`, but I have copy/pasted it into both rsample and dials without modification. It is useful to be able to call it directly to add the attributes of `to` back onto `x` (except names and row names)

- `<subclass>_reconstructable(x, to)` - This is the core logic of “I did some stuff to `x`, is it still a valid `<subclass>`?“. It returns a boolean.

- `<subclass>_maybe_reconstruct(x, to)` - This is a helper that involves all three of the above. If `x` is reconstructable to `to`, it calls `<subclass>_reconstruct()`, otherwise it calls `<subclass>_strip()`

The implementation of these in dials is all here
https://github.com/tidymodels/dials/blob/b876ade2ae5e6946ebea796ab93190fd54117394/R/compat-vctrs-helpers-parameters.R

---

It might be possible for some of this to live in vctrs:

- `df_downcast(x, remove = character())` and `tib_downcast(x, remove = character())` could replace `<subclass>_strip(x)`. They take a data frame, remove the `remove` attributes, then return a new bare df or tibble

- `df_reconstruct(x, to)` is pretty straightforward. It is exactly `dplyr_reconstruct.data.frame()` and could be optimized a bit more in C (is this just `vec_restore_default()`?)

Then I would really just need to create `<subclass>_reconstructable(x, to)`, which makes sense because it involves the logic specific to my subclass.

Then I use the combination of the above in the vctrs/dplyr methods, which isn’t _too_ bad.

title: Is `as.list.vctrs_rcrd()` required?
How to write.csv with vctrs data.frame
description:
The following gives an error for character casting.
```
  new_percent <- function(x = double()) {
    vec_assert(x, double())
    new_vctr(x, class = "vctrs_percent")
  }
  x <- new_percent(c(seq(0, 1, length.out = 4), NA))
  d <- data.frame(x)
  d
  write.csv(d, "~/Downloads/tmp.csv") # Error: Can't convert <vctrs_percent> to <character>.
```
In the previous version I was able to declare an explicit cast to character using `vec_cast` to be able to use write.csv with my custom vector types. The change log for 0.3.0 says: "vec_cast() no longer converts to character. Use as.character()to deparse objects."
But I have no idea how to do that from inside my vctrs package, without changing `write.csv` or making sure to use `as.character` in all my custom vector types before writing to disk the data.frame.

Any ideas?

title: Convenience promotion type from character to dates
description:
There should be a convenience common type so that this is allowed:

```r
x < "2000-01-01"
```

On the other hand, directional casting should probably only be allowed towards dates. This should be an error:

```r
map_chr(1:3, ~ Sys.Date())
```

Another type that has a convenience promotion type is `version`.

title: Is the `c()` fallback `name_spec` check too restrictive?
description:
In slider I was planning on calling `vec_unchop(out, .name_spec = zap())` from `slide_vec(.x, .f)`, where `out` is a list of size 1 results from repeatedly calling `.f` over the slices of `.x`.

I don't know the type of the contents of `out`, but I do know that I don't care about the vec-names of each element of `out`, so I want to zap them (the names of `.x` are used instead).

But since `out` could hold any type, I can't set `.name_spec = zap()` with the current strictness around the `.name_spec` because:

```r
library(vctrs)

foobar <- function(x = list()) {
  structure(x, class = "foobar")
}

c.foobar = function(...) {
  xs <- list(...)
  xs <- lapply(xs, unclass)
  out <- vec_unchop(xs)
  foobar(out)
}

vec_c(foobar(1), foobar(2), .name_spec = rlang::zap())
#> Error: Can't use a name specification with non-vctrs types.
#> vctrs methods must be implemented for class `foobar`.
#> See <https://vctrs.r-lib.org/articles/s3-vector.html>.
```

Maybe we can special case `zap()` here
https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/3dc326ac95b46eed9c75cade342aa96f3f415230/src/c.c#L212

And use `vec_set_names(out, R_NilValue)` on this if `name_spec = zap()`
https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/3dc326ac95b46eed9c75cade342aa96f3f415230/src/c.c#L205

title: Trying to understand how to use c() with a vctrs object
description:
Hi,

Apologies - I've asked around in both the RStudio forums and Stack overflow with no responses: I suspect this is because vctrs is still quite 'niche'.

I've read through the sample documentation, Earo Wang's blog tutorial and the RStudioConf tutorials.

I've started with what I thought would be the simplest case scenario (two character attributes - so basically a string, and a descriptor for that string).

I've built a constructor, new_toy_vector. I haven't built a convenience function in this example yet.

I then had trouble when I used c() on my object. Could anyone advise me what I'm missing here?

(Hoping this also helps with the documentation and examples for vctrs).


``` r
new_toy_vector <- function(
  x = character(),
  descriptor = character()) {
  
  vctrs::vec_assert(x,character())
  vctrs::vec_assert(descriptor, character())

  vctrs::new_vctr(x,
                  descriptor = descriptor,
                  class = "toy_vector")
}



format.toy_vector <- function(x, ...) {
  paste0(vctrs::vec_data(x)," is ", attr(x, "descriptor"))
}

obj_print_data.toy_vector <- function(x) {
  cat(format(x), sep = "\n")
}

c(new_toy_vector("Hello", "Foo"), new_toy_vector("World", "Bar"))
#> Error: No common type for `..1` <toy_vector> and `..2` <toy_vector>.
```

<sup>Created on 2020-04-26 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>


I had thought from reading the documentation that coercion with itself was supported by default. I tried to create a coercion with itself unless the default method wasn't defined for some reason:

``` r
> vec_ptype2.toy_vector.toy_vector <- function(x, y, ...) new_toy_vector()
> c(new_toy_vector("Hello", "Foo"), new_toy_vector("World", "Bar"))
Error: Can't convert <toy_vector> to <toy_vector>.
```

Any ideas what I'm missing or misunderstanding? Why can't I combine the two objects in the example?

title: Should vec_cbind() and vec_rbind() always return class of first container?
description:
Before we consider implementations of other approaches, I think we need to carefully consider if it would be ok for `vec_rbind(x, y)` and `vec_cbind(x, y)` to always return the container type of `x` (provided that `x` is already a container). The primary advantage of this approach is simplicity — it's extremely easy for us to explain the underlying principle, maintainers of data frame extensions don't need to do anything, and it's simple to implement.

I think this principle is more appealing for row and column binding than vector concatenation because (essentially) all containers have the same base class (`data.frame()`).

vec_rbind() enforces row names when input is a named list
description:
When passing in a named list of data frames without row names to `vec_rbind()` the return value is a data frame with row names. This change can potentially trigger a hard-to-debug renaming message, e.g.

```r

vctrs::vec_rbind(!!!dfs)
#> New names:
#> * a -> a...1
#> * a -> a...2
#>       x
#> a...1 1
#> a...2 1
```

title: Coercion documentation
description:
When reading this https://vctrs.r-lib.org/reference/theory-faq-coercion.html, found "Type compatibility" and "Richness of type" sections confusing. Primarily, the notion of "richer"/"rich" is ambiguous/changing when referring to 1d vectors and 2d data frames (acknowledged in the FAQ).

The `factor` vs `character` 1d example suggests that `character` is richer (general) than `factor` (specific), and hence a combination of two results in `character` (general). However, this  rationale doesn't hold for the following 2d example `data.table` (specific) vs `data.frame` (general), because we should choose richer behaviours instead of richer data. I could probably argue `factor` is richer in behaviours than `character`, since `factor` owns the `level()`. 

I'm not sure `data.table` vs `data.frame` is a good example (neither `tbl_df` vs `data.frame`). Would be `grouped_df` vs `data.frame` a better alternative? Any reason on `vec_ptype2(<grouped_df>, <data.frame>)` returns `<grouped_df>`? I think `data.frame` is richer than `grouped_df`, because it's more flexible with fewer attributes/constraints.

For 1d, we should choose a more general type, but 2d goes with a more specific type?

title: vec_as_names not quiet when function is provided
description:
According to docs in vctrs 0.2.4,
```
By default, the user is informed of any renaming caused by repairing the names.
 This only concerns unique and universal repairing. Set quiet to TRUE to silence the messages.
```
yet it also prints the message when providing  custom function.i

```r
vctrs::vec_as_names(c("a", "b"), repair = function(x) paste0(x, 
    "a"), quiet = FALSE)
#> New names:
#> * a -> aa
#> * b -> ba
#> [1] "aa" "ba"
```
Should the docs be changed to match the behavior, or the behavior to match the docs?

title: vec_rbind() fails for subclasses of tibble()
description:
Hi team!

@elinw and I are updating [ropensci/skimr](https://www.github.com/ropensci/skimr) for the dplyr v1 release. We are struggling with the behavior of `vec_rbind()`. 
https://github.com/ropensci/skimr/issues/582

We use a `skim_df` object which inherits from a tibble.

```
library(skimr)
skimmed <- skimr::skim(iris)
str(skimmed)
#> tibble [5 × 15] (S3: skim_df/tbl_df/tbl/data.frame)
#>  $ skim_type        : chr [1:5] "factor" "numeric" "numeric" "numeric" ...
```

```
)

  factor.ordered   : logical
  factor.n_unique  : integer

```

I've tried some of the ptype logic, but it doesn't seem to solve it unless I provide a fully enumerated list of columns.

```
 skim_df <- function(...) {
   structure(
     tibble::tibble(...),
     class = c("skim_df", "tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"),
     data_rows = integer(),
     data_cols = integer(),
     df_name = character(),
     groups = list(),
     base_skimmers = character(),
     skimmers_used = list()
   )
}

vctrs::vec_rbind(
  dplyr::select(skimmed, -n_missing),

)

Error: Can't convert from <skim_df<
```

I have been looking at users of vctrs, and I am not seeing example solutions to this problem. Do I need a `vec_ptype2()` method? 

This matter a lot to us, because our `partition()` function creates of list of `one_skim_df` objects that inherit from tibble, but usually have different sets of columns. We want to be able to join it back together.

description:
Hi,

I was tempted and did the upgrade to the development version of `dplyr` after reading a bit in the blog post from @Hadley released earlier this week. Unfortunately, this broke my existing script at two locations, once (so far I have to say) at a `dplyr::bind_rows` position and once at a `tidyr::pivot_longer` position.

During the upgrade of `dplyr` to the development version, `vctrs` was updated as well.

title: Simplify double dispatch registration and lookup
description:
Regarding #982, I wonder if we could simplify the registration by registering all methods for `vec_ptype2()` and `vec_cast()` in the vctrs namespace.

For instance you'd register `vec_ptype2.character.foobar` as a `character.foobar` method for `vec_ptype2` instead of a `foobar` method for `vec_ptype2.character`. It feels like this should work?

That would simplify the registration process because the left methods wouldn't need to be exported or registered at all. Since they are no longer evaluated, it also feels cleaner that they don't need to exist. There wouldn't be multiple namespaces involved in the dispatch or registration, making the whole system more transparent and easier to document and use.

description: The same way `rbind()` does. Avoids annoying/confusing messages when uninformative character row names are inadvertently created (e.g. by the `survey` package).

title: How to cast to container type?
Support for sfc lists
description:
From https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/issues/985#issuecomment-608260268.

Since we're moving away from unstructured dispatch, we need to implement special support for other mechanisms like `AsIs` wrappers. sfc lists might need special support, but the general mechanism that would support them isn't clear.

sfc is a bit special because combination of disparate geometry types like `sfc<point>` and `sfc<line>` falls back to an abstract geometry type `sfc<ANY>`, something we generally don't do in vctrs (like falling back to deparsing or chopping). Combinations with types outside the sfc hierarchy should still be an error.

A similar type to sfc is `list_of()`, and the abstract geometry list is like a `list()`. Maybe a first step towards supporting sfc would be to implement a variant of `list_of()` that falls back to list as soon as one element doesn't have a common type?

(Ideally combining a `sfc<polygon>` and a `sfc<multipolygon>` would return the latter. Combining with something that isn't compatible falls back to the abstract type `sfc<ANY>`. These more refined rules aren't implemented yet though.)

title: Should `vec_set_names()` only fallback to `names<-` if there is no proxy?
description:
See discussion in #526.

Currently `vec_set_names()` falls back to `names<-` if the object is classed. For `vctrs_vctr` objects, we want to bypass this and just set the `R_NamesSymbol`. One way we could do this is see if the object implements a `vec_proxy()` like we do with `[` and `vec_slice()`.

But we need to consider the case of POSIXlt. It implements a proxy (a data frame) but the names are stored in the `$year` column. How do we know they are there without using `names<-`?

If we rework POSIXlt to use a `.names` column in its proxy, how do we know from inside `vec_set_names()` that that column exists and is the thing we need to alter?

title: Discussion: Optimizing binary ops where one input is size 1
description:
I think that _eventually_ it would be useful to optimize the binary functions that currently recycle to a common size to instead only check for a common size and leave size 1 inputs un-recycled.

This issue should serve as a place to collect functions that could potentially benefit from this:

- [ ] `vec_in(needles, haystack)`
- [ ] `vec_match(needles, haystack)`
- [ ] `vec_compare(x, y)`
- [ ] `vec_equal(x, y)`

title: vec_get()
description:
As a complement to `vec_slice()` @romainfrancois and I have been discussing the utility of a function that would extract 1 observation, but would be more of an analog to `[[` than `[`. Possible implementation:
```r vec_rip <- function (x, i) { if (is.logical(i)) { i <- which(i) } stopifnot(is.integer(i) || is.character(i)) # this is new stopifnot(length(i) == 1L) if (is.null(x)) { NULL } else if (is.data.frame(x)) { out <- lapply(x, `[`, i) vec_restore(out, x) } else if (is_vector(x)) { d <- vec_dims(x) if (d == 1) { # this is all that changed? if (is.object(x)) { # x[i] x[[i]] } else { .subset2(x, i) # x[[i, drop = FALSE]] } } else if (d == 2) { x[i, , drop = FALSE] } else { miss_args <- rep(list(missing_arg()), d - 1) eval_bare(expr(x[i, !!!miss_args, drop = FALSE])) } } else { stop("`x` must be a vector", call. = FALSE) } } ```

It would function somewhat like: ``` r vec_rip(list(x = 1, y = 2), 1L) #> [1] 1 vec_slice(list(x = 1, y = 2), 1L) #> $x #> [1] 1 # Not sure about what these should do: vec_rip(mtcars, 1L) #> mpg cyl disp hp drat wt qsec vs am gear carb #> 1 21 6 160 110 3.9 2.62 16.46 0 1 4 4 vec_rip(matrix(1:12, nrow = 3), 1L) #> [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] #> [1,] 1 4 7 10 vec_slice(starwars$films, 1L) #> [[1]] #> [1] "Revenge of the Sith" "Return of the Jedi" #> [3] "The Empire Strikes Back" "A New Hope" #> [5] "The Force Awakens" vec_rip(starwars$films, 1L) #> [1] "Revenge of the Sith" "Return of the Jedi" #> [3] "The Empire Strikes Back" "A New Hope" #> [5] "The Force Awakens" # vec_rip() can only extract 1 observation at a time vec_slice(starwars$films, 1:2) #> [[1]] #> [1] "Revenge of the Sith" "Return of the Jedi" #> [3] "The Empire Strikes Back" "A New Hope" #> [5] "The Force Awakens" #> #> [[2]] #> [1] "Attack of the Clones" "The Phantom Menace" #> [3] "Revenge of the Sith" "Return of the Jedi" #> [5] "The Empire Strikes Back" "A New Hope" vec_rip(starwars$films, 1:2) #> Error in vec_rip(starwars$films, 1:2): length(i) == 1L is not TRUE ``` ~We are currently undecided on what it "should" do for data frames and matrices. A couple ideas:~ ~1) Return the 1 row observation as is (so the same as `vec_slice()`, this is shown above). This doesn't feel right. 2) Extract the 1 row observation, then coerce it to some lower level type. For data.frames, a list and for matrices, a vector.~ ~If `2)` is chosen, one question that came up is "what should it do for list columns"? Two possibilities:~ ``` r data("starwars", package = "dplyr") starwars <- starwars[,c("species", "films")] one_ob <- vctrs::vec_slice(starwars, 1L) # don't drop a dimension as.list(one_ob) #> $species #> [1] "Human" #> #> $films #> $films[[1]] #> [1] "Revenge of the Sith" "Return of the Jedi" #> [3] "The Empire Strikes Back" "A New Hope" #> [5] "The Force Awakens" # drop 1 dimension lapply(one_ob, .subset2, 1) #> $species #> [1] "Human" #> #> $films #> [1] "Revenge of the Sith" "Return of the Jedi" #> [3] "The Empire Strikes Back" "A New Hope" #> [5] "The Force Awakens" # but with better support for this # so it doesn't unravel (i.e. better support # for vctr rcrd types) .subset2(as.POSIXlt(Sys.time()), 1) #> [1] 26.99161 ```

title: Data-dependent attributes and `vec_assert`/`is_same_type` problem
description:
Hello, 

I am working on adapting the classes in one of my packages to use the `vctrs` package and it is working great so far. Its quite useful, thanks! However, I ran into a problem:

It seems that data-dependent attributes make `vec_assert` say that types are different, because they have different attributes. I made a minimal example below (taken from the vignette) that replicates the issue I am having with my more complicated classes:

``` r
library(vctrs)

# Create test class with data-dependent attributes
new_cached_sum <- function(x = double(), sum = 0L) {
  vec_assert(x, ptype = double())
  vec_assert(sum, ptype = double(), size = 1L)
  
  new_vctr(x, sum = sum, class = "vctrs_cached_sum")
}

cached_sum <- function(x = double()) { # Note the addition of "= double()" to make 0-length possible
  x <- vec_cast(x, double())
  new_cached_sum(x, sum(x))
}

obj_print_footer.vctrs_cached_sum <- function(x, ...) {
  cat("# Sum: ", format(attr(x, "sum"), digits = 3), "\n", sep = "")
}


# This works as expected...
vec_assert(cached_sum(), ptype = cached_sum())


# ...but this does not
vec_assert(cached_sum(1), ptype = cached_sum())
#> `cached_sum(1)` must be a vector with type <vctrs_cached_sum>.
#> Instead, it has type <vctrs_cached_sum>.


# because of this behavior of vec_assert
x <- cached_sum(1)
ptype <- cached_sum()
ptype <- vec_type(ptype)
x_type <- vec_type_finalise(vec_type(x))
vctrs:::is_same_type(x_type, ptype)
#> [1] FALSE
```

<sup>Created on 2019-06-20 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

This is an issue for me because I am trying to use the class with data-dependent attributes as an element in another record-style class and  `vec_assert` causes an error when the constructor is given the class with data-dependent attributes.

This is caused by this part of `vec_assert`:

https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/14c5fdfd8c319420d8936aa9a99fbc72a1ebc48c/R/assert.R#L40-L42

And the use of `identical` in `is_same_type` here:

https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/14c5fdfd8c319420d8936aa9a99fbc72a1ebc48c/R/assert.R#L120

Is this intended behavior? I am still a bit new to `vctrs`, so I might be missing something. Perhaps I should use "partial types" to solve this? I just came across "partial types"  in the code while debugging and reading the related issue https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/issues/261, but I dont really understand the concept yet. I cant tell if this is exactly the same issue as https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/issues/261, but they are very similar at least.

If it is intended behavior, the error message is confusing; it would be nice if the error message said that the types are the same, but the attributes differ or something like that.

title: Consider interface of vec_assert() and vec_is()
description:
Currently they handle type and size in a single function. This doesn't feel quite right because often you'll want to assert that the size is a constant, but coerce the type (or vice versa) and this makes the interface asymmetric. It might be better to have `vec_assert_size()` and `vec_assert_type()` to match `vec_recycle()` and `vec_cast()`.  (With `vec_assert_type(x)` presumably replacing `vec_assert(x))`).

With this interface we could consider specifying the comparator as either a value or a template, which would make it possible to generate more informative error messages:

```R
x <- 1:3
y <- 1:4

vec_asssert_size(x, value = 4)
#> Error: `x` must have size 3, not size 4.

vec_asssert_size(x, template = y)
#> Error: `x` must have the same size as `y`
```

title: vec_is() too strict for data frames that append to class?
description:
``` r

class(df) <- c("data.frame", "foo")

is.data.frame(df)
#> [1] TRUE
vctrs::vec_is(df)
#> [1] FALSE
```

<sup>Created on 2020-03-29 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

Appending the class can lead to undesired behavior for *existing* methods, but this is not necessarily wrong if the new class only implements own methods (mixin or multiple inheritance):

``` r
df <- data.frame(a = 1)
class(df) <- c("data.frame", "foo")

print.foo <- function(x, ...) {
  cat("Print overridden\n")
  invisible(x)
}

vctrs::s3_register("base::print", "foo")

# Not accessing overridden method:
df
#>   a
#> 1 1

# Works when reversing the class
class(df) <- c("foo", "data.frame")
df
#> Print overridden
```

title: vec_as_names repair = "universal" can be non-unique
description:
It is possible to receive non-unique names from `vec_as_names(..., repair = "universal")`as follows:

````r
> vctrs::vec_as_names(c("", "1"), repair = "universal", quiet = TRUE)
[1] "...1" "...1"
````

This could happen wherever empty strings and character representations of integers co-exist and the 'integer' corresponds to the position of the empty string. 

````r
> vctrs::vec_as_names(c("", "5", "a", "b", "", "1"), repair = "universal", quiet = TRUE)
[1] "...1" "...5" "a"    "b"    "...5" "...1"
````

The issue is that in the hierarchy of `minimal` < `unique` < `universal` the logic of making character representations of integers `universal` undermines the logic applied to make empty strings `unique`. Everything is fine at the `unique`-only stage:

````r
> vctrs::vec_as_names(c("", "1"), repair = "unique", quiet = TRUE)
[1] "...1" "1"
````

Apologies if this is known and I have just missed it. But at the least this seems counter to the docs ("`universal` names are `unique` and syntactic...") and doesn't seem to be mentioned as a known issue in the [design guide](https://principles.tidyverse.org/names-attribute.html). At the least, this seems worthy of a mention as an edge case?

title: Devel vctrs::vec_rbind does not remove column names in list columns
description:
This is breaking behavior for https://github.com/colearendt/tidyjson, so wanted to report it. It is not clear to me whether this is an intentional or unintentional change in behavior. It seems marginally related to #999 and #966. 

As I think about this behavior, it seems almost desirable to keep the names - it was not clear to me why names were dropped in the first place (but we do depend on it in a few places, for better or worse. Others may as well).

I originally noticed the behavior in `tidyr::unnest()` and traced it here:

### original behavior
Notice that `chr "b"` is not named
``` r
packageVersion("vctrs")
#> [1] '0.2.4'
hm <- tibble::tibble(col = list(a = "b"))
str(vctrs::vec_rbind(hm, .ptype = NULL))
#> tibble [1 × 1] (S3: tbl_df/tbl/data.frame)
#>  $ col:List of 1
#>   ..$ : chr "b"
```

<sup>Created on 2020-04-13 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

### devel behavior
Notice that `chr "b"` retains its name
``` r
packageVersion("vctrs")
#> [1] '0.2.99.9011'
hm <- tibble::tibble(col = list(a = "b"))
str(vctrs::vec_rbind(hm, .ptype = NULL))
#> tibble [1 × 1] (S3: tbl_df/tbl/data.frame)
#>  $ col:List of 1
#>   ..$ a: chr "b"
```

<sup>Created on 2020-04-13 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

title: vec_size() takes a "long time" for POSIXlt
description:
``` r
library(vctrs)

ct <- new_datetime(0)
lt <- as.POSIXlt(ct)

bench::mark(
  vec_size(ct),
  vec_size(lt)
)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression        min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>   <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 vec_size(ct)    727ns    944ns  1013283.     6.3KB    101. 
#> 2 vec_size(lt)   18.6µs   21.8µs    42695.    29.5KB     25.6
```

Discovered while repeatedly calling `vec_restore(x, to, R_NilValue)` where `x` was a list holding a POSIXlt and `to` was a data frame. Because no size was passed in, it goes through `df_raw_size(x)`, which in this case calls `vec_size()` on the first element of the list (the POSIXlt). Totally crippled performance 😬 . Luckily I am able to pre-compute the size ahead of time to fix it for my use case.

The main "issue" is that `vec_size()` needs the proxy:
https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/f736b2353d248820847a09b808cb7370ab8fc2f6/src/size.c#L47

and `vec_proxy.POSIXlt` calls `new_data_frame()`, which is quite slow:

``` r
library(vctrs)

ct <- new_datetime(0)
lt <- as.POSIXlt(ct)

# imitate vec_proxy.POSIXlt
vctrs:::vec_proxy.POSIXlt
#> function(x, ...) {
#>   new_data_frame(unclass(x))
#> }
#> <bytecode: 0x7f99f69716f8>
#> <environment: namespace:vctrs>

# no problem here:
bench::mark(unclass(lt))
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   expression       min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>  <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 unclass(lt)    308ns    373ns  2350164.        0B     235.

lt_unclassed <- unclass(lt)

# ouch
bench::mark(new_data_frame(lt_unclassed))
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   expression                       min  median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>                   <bch:t> <bch:t>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 new_data_frame(lt_unclassed)  14.9µs  17.6µs    52643.    24.8KB     15.8
```

Perhaps there is no solution, since we have to get the full proxy, but this is definitely something to be aware of when liberally using `vec_size()` and expecting it to have negligible speed impacts.

title: `as.list.vctrs_vctr()` with list vctrs
description:
Can we revisit the behavior of `as.list.vctrs_vctr()`? 

https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/1893f3526b87fa87b4f6a5430e8f3509a5b29be6/R/type-vctr.R#L282-L290

I don't think it needs to special case lists, I think `vec_chop()` does (nearly) the right thing.

``` r
library(vctrs)

x <- new_vctr(list(1, 2))

# lost the class?
as.list(x)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] 2


vec_chop(x)
#> [[1]]
#> <vctrs_vctr[1]>
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> <vctrs_vctr[1]>
#> [1] 2

# this looks right to me
vec_chop(x)[[1]]
#> <vctrs_vctr[1]>
#> [1] 1
unclass(vec_chop(x)[[1]])
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 1
```

<sup>Created on 2020-04-14 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

The `package_version` class is a vector that is internally a list, and does what I am proposing

```r
# internally this is a list
y <- package_version(c("1.0.0", "1.0.1"))

unclass(y)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 1 0 0
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] 1 0 1

# keeps class, splits into size 1 elements of that class
as.list(y)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] '1.0.0'
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] '1.0.1'
```

The only thing is that `vec_chop()` should really be `vec_chop2()`, and names on the object should be lost (I think this is a property of `as.*()` functions generally. It can be fixed in the short term with

```r
as.list.vctrs_vctr <- function(x) {
  # TODO: replace with `vec_chop2()`
  x <- vec_set_names(x, NULL)
  vec_chop(x)
}
```

title: vec_as_index() improvements
description:
Lessons learned from tibble.

1. Should `vec_slice()` be allowed to extend the vector?

    We should keep the following invariant: `` `vec_slice<-`(x, i, value)`` is the same as `` `vec_slice<-`(x, vec_as_index(i, vec_size(x), names2(x)), value)`` . 

2. Do we need `vec_as_scalar_index()` ? This would have the same semantics as `vec_as_index()` but only support positive scalar numerics and scalar names.

3. Do we really need both the `n` and the `names` argument to `vec_as_index()` and `vec_as_position()`? Can we allow a character vector as the `n` argument?

To be continued.

It is private to getNamespace("vctrs") so that would be ok (but dangerous).  The only call to it in the R and src directories supplies the name, but the tests are full of calls to it without the tags.  E.g., 

vctrs/tests/testthat/test-compare.R:  expect_equal(vec_order(data_frame(list(10, 2, 1))), 1:3)

It would be nice if it produced a valid data.frame so that functions that depend on data.frames having names worked.

I see the public vctrs::new_data_frame can also make a data.frame without names.  Should this be allowed?

title: A clarification on `vec_match()` with attributes
description:
What is the correct behavior of `vec_match()` when attributes are involved? Consider a few base R examples:

- When the names are on the outermost vector, they are ignored.
- When the names are on the inner elements of a list, they are important since R calls `as.character()` on the inputs when they are lists.

``` r
x <- c(x_nm = 1)
y <- c(y_nm = 1)

match(x, y)
#> [1] 1

match(list(x), list(y))
#> [1] NA

as.character(list(x))
#> [1] "c(x_nm = 1)"

as.character(list(y))
#> [1] "c(y_nm = 1)"
```

Notice this has inconsistent behavior though. Consider what happens with characters. Notice how the `as.character()` call doesn't retain the names, so things look equal.

``` r
x <- c(x_nm = "1")
y <- c(y_nm = "1")

match(x, y)
#> [1] 1

match(list(x), list(y))
#> [1] 1

as.character(list(x))
#> [1] "1"

as.character(list(y))
#> [1] "1"
```

With other attributes, they are ignored (as far as i can tell) when converting to character.

``` r
x <- 1
x_attr <- structure(1, stuff = 1)

match(x, x_attr)
#> [1] 1

match(list(x), list(x_attr))
#> [1] 1

as.character(list(x))
#> [1] "1"

as.character(list(x_attr))
#> [1] "1"
```

What should `vec_match()` do? There are really two questions:

- Should names and attributes be ignored with this? My gut reaction is yes.

```r
vec_match(c(x_nm = 1), c(y_nm = 1))
#> [1] 1
```

- Should names and attributes be ignored in the nested version? My gut reaction is no.

```r
vec_match(list(c(x_nm = 1)), list(c(y_nm = 1)))
#> [1] NA
```

Similar questions arise with `vec_equal()` on these same examples.

title: Make `vec_cast()` a directional coercion generic
description:
There are two issues with the current casting rules in vctrs:

- They make vctrs complicated. Users and class implementors need to know about two diagrams for coercions and casts.

- The casting rules do not seem to be the right default most of the time. For instance input validation can't use `vec_cast()` because it is too flexible.

To fix this, we could make `vec_cast()` a directional coercion. 

- A __non-directional__ coercion converts an object to the common type, which is always the larger type (i.e. integer is coerced to double).

- A __directional__ coercion converts an object to the type supplied by the caller, but only if there exists a common type. A directional coercion is no longer guaranteed to convert to the larger type. If the cast is lossy, this is an error by default, unless the code is wrapped in `vctrs::allow_lossy_cast()`.

Essentially, we'd add the rule that `vec_cast()` methods can only be implemented for coercible types, i.e. types that have a common type specified by `vec_ptype2()` methods.

### Cast methods to remove

It is unclear yet how much of a breaking change it would be to remove these methods, we might need a deprecation strategy:

- character casts
- list casts
- double <-> date

Where should this conversion logic go? Either we move it to separate single-dispatch generics like `vec_as_double()`, or we add a new double-dispatch generic in vctrs. @davisvaughan suggested the name `vec_force()`.

- Even if we have a double-dispatch generic, it is nice to have the explicit is_ and as_ functions for a class, so we might end up with separate wrappers anyway.

- The separate generics have the advantage of requiring only a single dispatch, which makes things faster for users and simpler for class authors.

- At a syntax level, having a single double-dispatch generic seems to give a false sense of principled genericity, whereas most of the implemented behaviour is ad hoc.

- On the other hand, `vec_force()` could be useful as part of a deprecation plan.

title: Prevent `vec_cast()` methods from being inherited
description:
I think this is similar to https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/pull/742

In rray I have tests for:

```r
test_that("from unknown types", {
  expect_error(vec_cast("chr", rray(1)), class = "vctrs_error_incompatible_cast")
  expect_error(vec_cast(rray(1), "chr"), class = "vctrs_error_incompatible_cast")
})
```

With dev vctrs I get:

``` r
library(rray)
library(vctrs)

vec_cast("chr", rray(1))
#> Error: Can't cast `x` <character> to `to` <rray<dbl>>.

vec_cast(rray(1), "chr")
#> <rray<dbl>[1]>
#> [1] "1"
```

I think that we need `vec_cast.character.double()` to include the same `is.object()` check as `vec_ptype2()` methods for base types. So I imagine it would become something like:

```r
vec_cast.character.double <- function(x, to, ...) {
  if (is.object(x)) {
    vec_default_cast(x, to) # x_arg, y_arg?
  } else {
    x <- vec_coerce_bare(x, "character")
    shape_broadcast(x, to)
  }
}
```

title: `vec_is_na()` / `vec_are_na()`
description:
Needed for detecting missing elements when input is potentially a tibble. Cf https://github.com/lionel-/recode/commit/c4e6b9b

```r
vec_are_na <- function(x) {
  vec_equal(x, vec_init(x, vec_size(x)), na_equal = TRUE)
}
```

Probably needs a fast native implementation.

Do we want to follow the rlang experiment with vectorised predicates, and use `are` instead of `is`? I think a good rule is that any `is_` function must be usable as an `if ()` condition, i.e. only return a single `TRUE` or `FALSE`, never a missing value or a length > 1 vector. title: `new_data_frame()` attribute issues
description:
strips names if you provide extra attributes

``` r
library(vctrs)

new_data_frame(list(x = 1), n = 1L, stuff = "foo")
#>    
#> 1 1
```

won't let you add row names

``` r
library(vctrs)

row.names(new_data_frame(list(x = 1), n = 1L, row.names = "y"))
#> [1] "1"
```

I think the ordering of how attributes are added is a little off. The `SET_ATTRIB()` call will nuke all existing attributes, including names. So we could special case names by holding onto them and restoring them after calling that.

For manually added row names, currently they are added by the `SET_ATTRIB()` call, but then nuked by the `new_data_frame()` call.

title: vec_match() and NA matching
description:
`dplyr` join functions internally use `vec_match()` now, but `vec_match()` always match NA, we need some way to implement `*_join(..., na_matches = "never")` 

```r
test_that("NAs match in joins only with na_matches = 'na' (#2033)", {
  skip("until vctrs can power na_matches = 'never'")

  df1 <- tibble(a = NA)
  df2 <- tibble(a = NA, b = 1:3)
  for (na_matches in c("na", "never")) {
    accept_na_match <- (na_matches == "na")
    expect_equal(inner_join(df1, df2, na_matches = na_matches) %>% nrow(), 0 + 3 * accept_na_match)
    expect_equal(left_join(df1, df2, na_matches = na_matches) %>% nrow(), 1 + 2 * accept_na_match)
    expect_equal(right_join(df2, df1, na_matches = na_matches) %>% nrow(), 1 + 2 * accept_na_match)
    expect_equal(full_join(df1, df2, na_matches = na_matches) %>% nrow(), 4 - accept_na_match)
    expect_equal(anti_join(df1, df2, na_matches = na_matches) %>% nrow(), 1 - accept_na_match)
    expect_equal(semi_join(df1, df2, na_matches = na_matches) %>% nrow(), 0 + accept_na_match)
  }
})
```

title: Working with the `vec_assign_impl()` callable
description:
So in {slide} I use `vec_assign_impl(clone = false)` for building up my output container, which works great for the most part. But it doesn’t capture the case where the output container is a matrix / we don’t have a proxy method, because in those cases we fall back to `vec_assign_fallback()` earlier in `vec_assign()`, not in `vec_assign_impl()`
https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/8d12bfc0e29e056966e0549af619253253752a64/src/slice-assign.c#L46

This means that tests like these fail for me in `slide_vec()`, where the output container could be a matrix
https://github.com/DavisVaughan/slide/blob/a070c3025a88904348b302a7a77d2cfad0d52aa0/tests/testthat/test-slide-vec.R#L106

I see two possible solutions:

- We move this check into `vec_assign_impl()`, but that seems odd because if I set `clone = false` and we do have to fallback, because I’m not sure if it would work right (would it clone anyways?).
- I have to do this check myself in {slide}. That means I would need `vec_proxy_info()` and `vec_assign_fallback()` callables. And I guess I’d have to know how to work with the return value of a `struct vctrs_proxy_info` in slide.

title: [Use case] Decorated file paths
description:
I am trying to create a data type that behaves like a character vector but secretly keeps track of a hash for each element. Is there a workaround, or is it too much of an edge case?

The hash is important for https://github.com/ropensci/drake/issues/1168, and I would like to generalize the idea for https://github.com/ropensci/drake/issues/1112. Record-style objects almost work, but I am having trouble emulating all the desired character-like behavior (see below). Maybe users just need to call `as.character()` themselves, but that is friction I would prefer to avoid if possible.

I thought about simply using `new_vctr("filename", hash = "hash_of_file", class = "ref_file")` and a `vec_restore()` method, but `c()` and friends remove the hash attribute, and restoring file hashes (with `vec_restore()` and `digest::digest()`) would be expensive.

``` r
ref_file <- function(...) {
  path <- as.character(c(...))
  hash <- purrr::map_chr(path, digest::digest, file = TRUE)
  new_ref_file(path = path, hash = hash)
}

new_ref_file <- function(path = character(0), hash = character(0)) {
  vctrs::vec_assert(path, ptype = character())
  vctrs::vec_assert(hash, ptype = character())
  vctrs::new_rcrd(fields = list(path = path, hash = hash), class = "ref_file")
}

format.ref_file <- function(x, ...) {
  vctrs::field(x, "path")
}

vec_ptype2.ref_file <- function(x, y, ...) UseMethod("vec_ptype2.ref_file", y)
vec_ptype2.ref_file.default <- function(x, y, ..., x_arg = "x", y_arg = "y") {
  vec_default_ptype2(x, y, x_arg = x_arg, y_arg = y_arg)
}
vec_ptype2.ref_file.ref_file <- function(x, y, ...) new_ref_file()
vec_ptype2.ref_file.character <- function(x, y, ...) new_ref_file()
vec_ptype2.character.ref_file <- function(x, y, ...) new_ref_file()
vec_cast.ref_file <- function(x, to, ...) UseMethod("vec_cast.ref_file")
vec_cast.ref_file.default <- function(x, to, ...) vec_default_cast(x, to)
vec_cast.ref_file.ref_file <- function(x, to, ...) x
vec_cast.character.ref_file <- function(x, to, ...) vctrs::field(x, "path")
vec_cast.ref_file.character <- function(x, to, ...) ref_file(x)

files <- fs::file_create(c(tempfile(), tempfile(), tempfile()))
purrr::walk(files, function(x) writeLines(x, x))
ref <- ref_file(files)

# ✓ data
vctrs::field(ref, "path")
#> [1] "/var/folders/k3/q1f45fsn4_13jbn0742d4zj40000gn/T/Rtmp970LBS/file73d55548986e"
#> [2] "/var/folders/k3/q1f45fsn4_13jbn0742d4zj40000gn/T/Rtmp970LBS/file73d5110f8980"
#> [3] "/var/folders/k3/q1f45fsn4_13jbn0742d4zj40000gn/T/Rtmp970LBS/file73d5130c3b40"
vctrs::field(ref, "hash")
#> [1] "e10c29578e76aef90d7558aa2f24b890" "d12e00e1c10374f86d21c1394da44793"
#> [3] "bccb3416fe56be7d4b38b35820b0c03c"

# ✓ printing
ref
#> <ref_file[3]>
#> [1] /var/folders/k3/q1f45fsn4_13jbn0742d4zj40000gn/T/Rtmp970LBS/file73d55548986e
#> [2] /var/folders/k3/q1f45fsn4_13jbn0742d4zj40000gn/T/Rtmp970LBS/file73d5110f8980
```

title: Revisit special casing of `vec_ptype2.logical.list()`
description:
See https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/pull/812#discussion_r379065426

`vec_ptype2.logical.list()` was special cased to not allow `vec_assign(list(1), 1, NA)`, but `vec_assign(list(1), 1, unspecified(1))` happened to slip through because it isn't caught by that method. This special case complicates the `vec_type2()` C code and is why I need `vec_ptype2_dispatch_unspecified_list()`.

I personally think that `vec_assign(list(1), 1, NA)` should be allowed, and is well defined. `NA` is cast to `list(NULL)`, and then assigned.

So my suggestion would be to:

- Remove `vec_ptype2.logical.list()` entirely, and let `vec_ptype2.logical.default()` be called

- Remove the C level `vec_ptype2_dispatch_unspecified_list()` special case (remove C level `stop_incompatible_type()` if we do this)

- Update the test in `test-slice-assign.R` to allow `NA` to be assigned into lists (and continue monitoring the existing test that `unspecified()` can also be assigned into lists)

title: Request: Native support for bare tibbles in `vec_ptype2()`
description:
I think eventually the plan is to support bare tibbles in `vec_ptype2()`, so we don't have to dispatch to `vec_ptype2.tbl_df.data.frame()` when we have two tibbles.

I just wanted to open this issue saying that we could get some really nice performance benefits from doing this that would carry over into all aspects of vctrs (and tidyr), especially `vec_rbind()`.

See that checking the `vec_ptype2()` of two data frames is much faster than two tibbles

``` r
library(vctrs)
library(tibble)

df <- data.frame(x = 1, y = 2)
tbl <- as_tibble(df)

bench::mark(
  vec_ptype2(df, df),
  vec_ptype2(tbl, tbl),
  check = FALSE
)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression                min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>           <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 vec_ptype2(df, df)     3.27µs   3.98µs   239273.    1.95KB     47.9
#> 2 vec_ptype2(tbl, tbl)  11.58µs  13.19µs    74161.     5.7KB     74.2
```

Most of the overhead is in the method dispatch

```r
vec_ptype2_tbl_df_data.frame <- vctrs:::vec_ptype2.tbl_df.data.frame

bench::mark(
  vec_ptype2(tbl, tbl),
  vec_ptype2_tbl_df_data.frame(tbl, tbl)
)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression                                min  median `itr/sec` mem_alloc
#>   <bch:expr>                             <bch:> <bch:t>     <dbl> <bch:byt>
#> 1 vec_ptype2(tbl, tbl)                   8.59µs 11.48µs    81208.        0B
#> 2 vec_ptype2_tbl_df_data.frame(tbl, tbl) 2.81µs  3.21µs   288311.        0B
#> # … with 1 more variable: `gc/sec` <dbl>
```

This has significant impact when we do something like rbind a large list of data frames together.

```r
lst_df <- rep(list(df), 100000)
lst_tbl <- rep(list(tbl), 100000)

bench::mark(
  vec_ptype_common(!!! lst_df),
  vec_ptype_common(!!! lst_tbl),
  check = FALSE
)
#> Warning: Some expressions had a GC in every iteration; so filtering is
#> disabled.
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression                        min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc
#>   <bch:expr>                   <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>
```

title: vec_ptype2.unspecified.integer64() is never used
description:

Luckily `vec_ptype()` works on `integer64()` objects, so we get correct results anyways

title: Record-style objects incompatible with dplyr::mutate ?
description:
Following the [vctrs vignette](https://vctrs.r-lib.org/articles/s3-vector.html#record-style-objects) about creating custom vector classes, I created the `rational` vector class. However, I found that `dplyr::mutate()` raises an error when applying transformations that return another `rational` vector.

It looks like `mutate()` is comparing the number of rows (expected outcome) to the number of columns in the record. Please see the example code below:

``` r
library(vctrs)
library(zeallot)
library(tidyverse)

new_rational <- function(n = integer(), d = integer()) {
  vec_assert(n, ptype = integer())
  vec_assert(d, ptype = integer())
  
  new_rcrd(list(n = n, d = d), class = "vctrs_rational")
}

rational <- function(n, d) {
  c(n, d) %<-% vec_cast_common(n, d, .to = integer())
  c(n, d) %<-% vec_recycle_common(n, d)
  
  new_rational(n, d)
}

format.vctrs_rational <- function(x, ...) {
  n <- field(x, "n")
  d <- field(x, "d")
  
  out <- paste0(n, "/", d)
  out[is.na(n) | is.na(d)] <- NA
  
  out
}

vec_arith.vctrs_rational <- function(op, x, y, ...) {
  UseMethod("vec_arith.vctrs_rational", y)
}
vec_arith.vctrs_rational.default <- function(op, x, y, ...) {
  stop_incompatible_op(op, x, y)
}

vec_arith.vctrs_rational.integer <- function(op, y, x, ...) {
  switch(
    op,
    "*" = new_rational(vec_arith_base(op, x, field(y, "n")), field(y, "d")),
    stop_incompatible_op(op, x, y)
  )
}

rational(1, 1:10) * 2L
#> <vctrs_rational[10]>
#>  [1] 2/1  2/2  2/3  2/4  2/5  2/6  2/7  2/8  2/9  2/10

tibble(x = rational(1, 1:10)) %>%
  mutate(y = x * 2L)
#> Error: Column `y` must be length 10 (the number of rows) or one, not 2
```

<sup>Created on 2020-02-16 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

title: vec_cast() with factors when `to` has no levels
description:
The current implementation of `vec_cast.factor.factor()` special cases when `to` has 0 levels, allowing you to do:

``` r
x <- factor(c("x", "y"))
x
#> [1] x y
#> Levels: x y

to <- factor()

vctrs:::vec_cast.factor.factor(x, to)
#> [1] x y
#> Levels: x y
```

<sup>Created on 2020-02-05 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0.9000)</sup>

I think this is too flexible? This feels like it would actually be the job of casting to a `partial_factor()`, and casting to a `factor()` should be more strict (you get the levels in `to` or die trying). We haven't fully implemented the `partial_factor()` cast methods but we could add them in to support being able to do this.

title: vec_cast() with factors and NA levels
description:
`factor()` has this interesting `exclude = NA` argument that excludes `NA` values from being set as `levels` by default. This results in _losing_ the `NA` factor level when a user casts to a factor that actually does have NA levels.

``` r
x <- factor(c("x", NA), exclude = NULL)
x
#> [1] x    <NA>
#> Levels: x <NA>

vctrs:::vec_cast.factor.factor(x, x)
#> [1] x    <NA>
#> Levels: x
```

<sup>Created on 2020-02-05 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0.9000)</sup>

I would argue that if you are casting `to` something with explicit `NA` levels, then those should stick around.

title: list_of loses type information?
description:
It looks like `list_of` does not correctly handle `vctrs_rcrd`-derived types.
When printing `list_of<test_record>`, while the type of list is correct, list items are treated as `vctrs_rcrd` base type instead of `test_record` derived type. As a result, printing fails, because `vctrs` explicitly throws in `format.vctrs_rcrd` and custom-defined `format.test_record` is never called.

``` r
new_record <- function(i = integer()) {
    vctrs::new_rcrd(list(i = i), class = "test_record")
}

format.test_record <- function(x, ...) paste0("i = ", vctrs::field(x, "i"))

new_record(5)
#> <test_record[1]>
#> [1] i = 5

vctrs::vec_ptype(new_record())
#> <test_record[0]>

class(new_record())
#> [1] "test_record" "vctrs_rcrd"  "vctrs_vctr"

vctrs::vec_ptype(vctrs::list_of(new_record(5)))
#> <list_of<test_record>[0]>

vctrs::list_of(new_record(5))
#> <list_of<test_record>[1]>
#> [[1]]
#> <vctrs_rcrd[1]>
#> Error: `format.vctrs_rcrd()` not implemented.

packageDescription("vctrs")[c("Version", "RemoteSha")]
#> $Version
#> [1] "0.2.99.9005"
#> 
#> $RemoteSha
#> [1] "4de029757dc9493586555f1026db3f12a4a34908"
```

title: Subsetting with `NULL`
description:
Just want to confirm something about `vec_as_location()`. `vec_as_index()` used to allow `NULL`. Is this expected behavior now?

```r
vctrs::vec_as_location(NULL, n = 1)
#> Error: Must subset with a proper subscript vector.
#> x `i` has the wrong type `NULL`.
#> ℹ These indices must be indicators, locations or names.
```

It looks like tibble is working around this, and its breaking some rray tests
https://github.com/tidyverse/tibble/blob/413e6e4ba1eac1a8b5ff3674696da912a36209ed/R/subsetting.R#L172

Confirming CRAN vctrs results:

```r
> vctrs::vec_as_index(NULL, 1L)
integer(0)
```

It looks like the old behavior treats `NULL` like `integer()`. If we were consistent with “`NULL` is a missing argument” then I guess `x[NULL]` should be treated as `x[]`.

We are actually a bit inconsistent in the dev version because this is allowed:

```r
> vctrs::vec_slice(1:2, NULL)
integer(0)
```

^ this happens because `vec_slice()` calls the C version of `vec_as_location()`, but the R version of `vec_as_location()` also goes through `vec_as_subscript()` which is where this is caught.

title: Library loading issues with dev tibble and vctrs
description:
I don't know exactly _why_ this happens, but I think I know a way to fix it. I'm more curious as to what's going on.

tibble used to use `@import vctrs`. If you have a version of tibble installed that does that, then you can `devtools::load_all()` vctrs with no problem.

tibble just recently switched to being more explicit, using `@importFrom vctrs ..fns..`. With the current dev tibble installed, I get this when loading vctrs with `load_all()`:

```r
> devtools::load_all(".")
Loading vctrs
Error: object ‘vec_slice<-’ is not exported by 'namespace:vctrs'
```

This isn't specific to `vec_slice<-`, it just happens to be `vec_slice<-` because of the order the imports are specified in tibble's `@importFrom` tags.

A traceback for the error sends me here, to where we call out to the tibble namespace in a test file (but not wrapped in a function)
https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/2e5416e759a65576e40daba9423c64fc95fb72f0/tests/testthat/helper-s3.R#L44

Wrapping that in a function like this seems to fix the issue

```r
tibble <- function(...) {
  tibble::tibble(...)
}
```

So I guess we can do that to fix it, I just don't know why the difference between `@import` and `@importFrom` was important.

title: Reviewing the subscript conversion UI
description:
The subscript/index conversion UI is challenging because it needs to be flexible enough to cover tidyselect, vctrs, and tibble usages. This is a proposal for making the naming more consistent and the functions more easily configurable. We'd rename:

```r
vec_coerce_index()    -> vec_as_subscript()
vec_as_index()        -> vec_as_location()

vec_coerce_location() -> vec_as_single_subscript()
vec_as_location()     -> vec_as_single_location()
```

The `as_location` functions convert to a numeric location in the vector. The `as_subscript` functions only convert to the base type of the three kinds of subscript vector:

* name → character
* indicator → logical
* location → integer (or double in the future when we add long vector support).

For example, factors are converted to character because all subtypes of characters are considered names.

`vec_as_subscript()` has options for ignoring or throwing an error for particular subscript types. `vec_as_location()` would have the same signature as `vec_as_subscript()`, with this definition:

```r
vec_as_location <- function(x,
                            n,
                            names = NULL,
                            indicator = c("convert", "error", "ignore"),
                            location = c("convert", "error", "ignore"),
                            name = c("convert", "error", "ignore")) {
  x <- vec_as_subscript(x, indicator = indicator, location = location, name = name)
  switch(typeof(x),
    logical = lgl_as_location(x, n, names),
    double = , # For long vectors
    integer = num_as_location(x, n, names),
    character = chr_as_location(x, n, names)
  )
}
```

It first calls `vec_as_subscript()` to get the base type, then calls specific conversion functions to convert to a numeric location. The specific conversion functions have additional options to control how values are converted:

```r
num_as_location <- function(x,
                            n,
                            names = NULL,
                            negative = c("invert", "error", "ignore"),
                            missing = c("error", "ignore")) {
  ...
}
num_as_single_location <- function(x,
                                   n,
                                   names = NULL,
                                   negative = c("error", "ignore"),
                                   missing = c("error", "ignore")) {
  ...
}
```

This is a departure from the current UI which tries to cram everything in `vec_as_location()` (currently called `vec_as_index()`). I think it's a good principle to split into multiple functions as soon as the parameters become trees (or flattened trees with prefixes).


`vec_as_index()` would go into a long deprecation cycle because it's used in CRAN tibble.

cc @DavisVaughan @hadley @krlmlr

title: list proxies behave differently than vectors with vec_init()
description:
Not sure if this is a bug or not (and seems possibly related to #445), but I discovered while developing a custom type that if you use a list as a proxy it will break `vec_init()`. I discovered this because I couldn't use `tidyr::pivot_wider()` with the type due to the usage of `vec_init()` inside `pivot_wider_spec()`. I assumed from the documentation of `vec_proxy()` that using a list as a proxy would be fine, but it seems to require a bit more care than I thought.

The actual type I'm developing is more complex than this example, but here is a reprex of a simple (and frankly kind of silly) type that just wraps around an internal vector as its first element:

``` r
library(tidyr)
library(vctrs)

new_a1 <- function(x) {
  new_vctr(list(x), class = "a1")
}

vec_proxy.a1 = function(x) {
  field(x, 1)
}

vec_restore.a1 = function(x, ...) {
  new_a1(x)
}

length.a1 = function(x, ...) {
  length(field(x, 1))
}

x1 = new_a1(c(1,2))
d1 = tibble(g = c("a", "b"), x = x1)
d1
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>   g         x
#>   <chr>  <a1>
#> 1 a         1
#> 2 b         2
pivot_wider(d1, names_from = g, values_from = x)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>       a     b
#>    <a1>  <a1>
#> 1     1     2
```

<sup>Created on 2019-11-05 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

I had assumed a similar type that uses a list as a proxy instead would also work, and for the most part it does --- except `pivot_wider` choked on it:

``` r
library(tidyr)
library(vctrs)

new_a2 <- function(x) {
  new_vctr(list(x), class = "a2")
}

vec_proxy.a2 = function(x) {
  as.list(field(x, 1))
}

vec_restore.a2 = function(x, ...) {
  new_a2(unlist(x))
}

length.a2 = function(x, ...) {
  length(field(x, 1))
}

x2 = new_a2(c(1,2))
d2 = tibble(g = c("a", "b"), x = x2)
d2
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>   g         x
#>   <chr>  <a2>
#> 1 a         1
#> 2 b         2
pivot_wider(d2, names_from = g, values_from = x)
#> Error: Can't index beyond the end of a vector.
#> The vector has length 0 and you've tried to subset element 1.
```

<sup>Created on 2019-11-05 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

I tracked the problem down to vec_init. vec_init works correctly on type a1:

```r
> vec_init(x1, 3)
<a1[3]>
[1] NA NA NA
```

But not on type a2:

```r
> vec_init(x2, 3)
<a2[0]>
```

This is because the proxy type for a2 is a list, and `vec_init()` is doing the equivalent of this:

```r
> vec_proxy(x2)[c(NA_integer_, NA_integer_, NA_integer_)]
[[1]]
NULL

[[2]]
NULL

[[3]]
NULL
```

Which after unlist yields `NULL`. A workaround I found was to change `vec_restore()` as follows:

```r
vec_restore.a2 = function(x, ...) {
  if (length(x) > 0) {
    x[sapply(x, is.null)] = NA
  }
  new_a2(unlist(x))
}
```

But I'm not sure if this represents a bigger potential issue, or if the problem should at least be documented for others who want to use lists as proxies.

title: Returning `list_of<>` vs `list` in "low level" functions
description:
I have a bit of a tough time deciding when to return a `list_of<>` from a vctrs function vs just a bare list. For example, `vec_chop()` returns a `list_of<>`:

``` r
vctrs::vec_chop(letters[1:2])
#> <list_of<character>[2]>
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "a"
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "b"
```

But this is slightly problematic because it is often used as a "low level" function where I really just want a bare list back. Like here in `as_df_row_impl()`

https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/2c8dd41312a8eadd7daf9729851ab1a50c667193/src/bind.c#L175

And here where I planned to implement `vec_cast.list.data.frame`

```r
vec_cast.list.data.frame <- function(x, to, ...) {
  row.names(x) <- NULL
  
  # returns list_of()
  out <- vec_chop(x)
  attributes(out) <- NULL
  
  # alternative - much slower
  #out <- map(vec_seq_along(x), vec_slice, x = x)
  
  out
}
```

@lionel- and I think that `vec_chop()` should just return a bare list, but we would like to be consistent about this and make a systematic change in all vctrs functions. For example, would it still make sense for `vec_split()` to return a `list_of<>`?

``` r
vctrs::vec_split(letters[1:4], c(1, 1, 2, 2))$val
#> <list_of<character>[2]>
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "a" "b"
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "c" "d"
```

@hadley what do you think about this?

title: vec_c does not correctly use proxy() for record vectors
description:
I am trying to implement a record vector in which the values are not necessarily stored in the vector class. Imagine a cached vector or file-based vector. In practice, this means that new_rcrd() is passed a field with some length not equal to the entire vector length. For example, new_rcrd() might have a field with a single vector of length 6, but the vector as a whole might be length 100. Other attributes would be passed to new_rcrd() to assist with reconstructing the whole vector. By calling vec_proxy(), a full-length vector can be reconstructed from the record. Other methods can be added as needed to handle indexing, length, etc.

This works well, with one exception. The function vec_c() does not work unless the .ptype is set to something other than the record vector class. So for example, vec_c(rcrd, rcrd, .ptype = integer()) works, while vec_c(rcrd, rcrd, .ptype = rcrd_class()) does not work and instead throws the error "Internal error in `vec_assign()`: `value` should have been recycled to fit `x`." Note that vec_assign() works fine in all cases when called as a stand-alone function. 

The problem seems to be that vec_c() is erroneously passing a record vector instead of the underlying proxy to vec_assign_impl() if the .ptype is a record vector class. I am not as well-versed in the underlying C code, but I think the key parts are (from vec_c in vctrs/c.c):

```
SEXP out = vec_init(ptype, out_size); # creates an empty record vector
PROTECT_WITH_INDEX(out, &out_pi);
out = vec_proxy(out); # gets the record vector proxy
...
SEXP x = VECTOR_ELT(xs, i); # gets the next element; which here would be a record vector
SEXP elt = PROTECT(vec_cast(x, ptype, args_empty, args_empty)); # casts the record vector to a record vector
...
vec_assign_impl(out, idx, elt, false); # assigns the record vector to the specified index of the record vector proxy. This causes an error, presumably because the elt record vector is erroneously unclassed and thus the length is wrong.
```

If my hunch is correct, then what should happen is that vec_assign_impl() in the above code should only be passed a vec_proxy(), something like:
`vec_assign_impl(out, idx, vec_proxy(elt), false)`

This would help with handling record vectors using vec_c. Thanks!

title: vec_unique() fails on lists of objects containing non-vectors
description:
In the current dev version, `vec_unique()` doesn’t work with lists of objects that are not vectors, or that contain non-vector elements in a recursive structure:

``` r
m <- glm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
vctrs::vec_unique(list(m, m))
#> Error: `x` must be a vector, not a `glm/lm` object

o <- list(x = expression(x))
vctrs::vec_unique(list(o, o))
#> Error: `x` must be a vector, not an expression vector
```

`glm` objects are an example of both, and can frequently appear in list columns in data frames. As `vec_unique()` gets more use behind the scenes in packages such as tidyr, this threatens to break code that works with list columns: e.g. https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/issues/735 seems to be a symptom of this behaviour.

title: Translation functions should be robust against scalar types
description:
Currently this fails:

``` r
vctrs::vec_unique(list(formula1 = Sepal.Length ~ Sepal.Width))
#> `x` must be a vector, not a `formula` object
```

The tidyr vignette does something like this. It used to work.

With the translation helpers, we call `vec_size()` on each list element to get the size, which causes the error for formulas. We should be robust against scalar types and just not translate them.

This is where the problem comes from

``` r
vctrs:::obj_maybe_translate_encoding(list(formula1 = Sepal.Length ~ Sepal.Width))
#> `x` must be a vector, not a `formula` object
```

I'm working on a PR for this now.

title: Performance: `vec_compare()`
description:
I think there could be a number of substantial improvements to `vec_compare()`

- Move the comparison loop in `vctrs_compare()` to be after the type check. So if we have a vector of ints it just checks that it is an integer once, and then loops through all of the values. This would use a similar approach as `vec_equal()`, but it will be made easier because we don't compare lists.

- Remove the `is_data_frame()`, length, and names checks from the `VECSXP` code path. This would probably require a switch to using `vec_proxy_typeof()` rather than `TYPEOF()` so we can know if we are in a data frame code path earlier on. These checks are pretty expensive, and we 100% don't need them because we called `vec_cast_common()` on the inputs already.

- Move the rest of the R side of `vec_compare()` to C. The only thing we need is the ability to call `vec_proxy_compare()` from the C level. Since we don't have a native implementation it could just call back to the R function.

- We also need to validate `na_equal`. i.e. this works when it shouldn't `vec_compare(1, 2, na_equal = list(1))`
