title: Dictionary functions should proxy inputs recursively
description:
I can bomb RStudio with this while in the vctrs project:

```r
devtools::load_all()
vec_unique_loc(data.frame(x = tuple(1:3, 1:3)))
```

There are two problems, both have to do with recursively proxying `x`.

---

The first problem is that we recursively call `vec_proxy_equal()` here
https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/2cce0f8c422e130cb270d95416724d107cc415e1/src/dictionary.c#L36

But we don't actually set `x` back to the proxied value. So when we `hash_fill()` it doesn't use the right version
https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/2cce0f8c422e130cb270d95416724d107cc415e1/src/dictionary.c#L61

It bombs because we try and pass along a df size of `3` here, but because the tuple is implemented as a list it only has a size of `2` when it hasn't been proxied (proxying it gives a data frame of size 3). It very much has to do with the FIXME note at the below link.
https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/2cce0f8c422e130cb270d95416724d107cc415e1/src/hash.c#L296

---

Second, it turns out that `obj_maybe_translate_encoding()` has essentially the same problem. It assumes we have recursively proxied and tries to pass along the data frame size when checking if any column need translation.
https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/2cce0f8c422e130cb270d95416724d107cc415e1/src/translate.c#L127

---

I think the best solution that fixes both problems is to recursively proxy in `vec_unique_loc()` and the other dictionary functions, rather than just calling `vec_proxy_equal()` once. There is no overhead in doing this since `init_dict()` does it anyways.

https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/2cce0f8c422e130cb270d95416724d107cc415e1/src/dictionary.c#L117

We could also recursively call `vec_proxy_equal()` in both `df_hash_fill()` and `obj_maybe_translate_encoding()`, which might be more robust if we use them elsewhere, but has the disadvantage that we'd be doing it twice.

title: `vec_unique()` makes a distinction between +0 and -0 while `unique()` does not
description:
Hi,

I noticed that vec_unique() seems to make a distinction between +0 and -0 while most R functions do not. This can affect the behavior of pivot_wider when +0 and -0 are present in the id_cols, causing it to generate two rows instead of one. 

This seems to be something about how the underlying C function vctrs_unique_loc() works, but that's as far as I got.

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(vctrs)

posZero = 0
negZero = ceiling(-0.9)

unique(posZero, negZero)
#> [1] 0
vec_unique(c(posZero, negZero ))
#> [1] 0 0

# using `abs()` to convert -0 to a +0 fixes the problem
vec_unique(abs(c(posZero, negZero)))
#> [1] 0

# Similarly, `identical()` normally treats these as equivalent
identical(posZero, negZero, num.eq = T)
#> [1] TRUE

# However, setting num.eq = F does a bitwise comparison and differentiates between +0 and -0
identical(posZero, negZero, num.eq = F)
#> [1] FALSE

# This can cause `pivot_wider()` to generate extra rows
data.frame(id = c(posZero, negZero),
           names = c('a', 'b'), 
           vals = c(1,2)) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = id, names_from =  names, values_from = vals )
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>      id     a     b
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     0     1    NA
#> 2     0    NA     2

# using `abs()` to convert the -0 to a +0 again fixes the problem
data.frame(id = c(posZero, negZero),
           names = c('a', 'b'), 
           vals = c(1,2)) %>%
  mutate(id = abs(id)) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = id, names_from =  names, values_from = vals )
#> # A tibble: 1 x 3
#>      id     a     b
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     0     1     2
```

<sup>Created on 2019-10-24 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

title: vec_ptype_common() cannot find a prototype when using (some) vectors created with {haven}
description:
Hi all,

`{haven}` is a tidyverse :package: allowing -- among other things -- to deal with labelled variables, which SPSS users are used to work with. There are a little like usual R factors except that the labels remain attributes and the numbers corresponding to each factors remain of class numeric or integer. Although converting such labelled numerical variables into factors is always an option, some users prefer to keep them as is to do arithmetic on such variables, which is a usual practice in social science (e.g. for the analysis of Likert scores).

Although not a high profile one, it would be great if it would play along with others tidyverse packages.  I've tracked a small limitation that seems to be caused by `vctrs::vec_ptype_common()`. This limitation has the unfortunate consequence of preventing pivoting tibbles:

``` r
library(tidyverse)

foo <- factor(c(1, 2))
bar <- factor(c(1, 3))

vctrs::vec_ptype_common(foo, bar)
#> factor(0)
#> Levels: 1 2 3

tibble(x = foo, y = bar) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything())
#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>   name  value
#>   <chr> <fct>
#> 1 x     1    
#> 2 y     1    
#> 3 x     2    
#> 4 y     3


foo <- haven::labelled(c(1, 2), labels = c(a = 1, b = 2))
bar <- haven::labelled(c(1, 3), labels = c(a = 1, c = 3))

vctrs::vec_ptype_common(foo, bar)
#> No common type for `..1` <haven_labelled> and `..2` <haven_labelled>.

tibble(x = foo, y = bar) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything())
#> No common type for `x` <haven_labelled> and `y` <haven_labelled>.
```

title: More dictionary + hashing + encoding issues
description:
*Sigh* - More encoding issues. 

``` r
library(vctrs)

string <- "\u00B0C"

utf <- iconv(string, from = Encoding(string), to = "UTF-8")
unknown <- iconv(string, from = Encoding(string), to = "", mark = FALSE)
latin1 <- iconv(string, from = Encoding(string), to = "latin1")

x <- list(utf = utf, unknown = unknown, latin1 = latin1)

# bad
vec_unique(x)
#> $utf
#> [1] "°C"
#> 
#> $unknown
#> [1] "°C"
#> 
#> $latin1
#> [1] "°C"

# good
vec_unique(unlist(x))
#>  utf 
#> "°C"
```

This affects _all_ functions in `dictionary.c` except `vec_match()` and `vec_in()`.

The reason this currently fails for the list is because the code path looks like:

`vec_unique` -> `init_dict_impl` -> `hash_fill` -> sees a list -> for each list element call `hash_object`

Each list element is a character vector, but when `hash_object()` eventually calls `chr_hash()` on each one, which checks if a translation is required, they can't "see" each other, so it thinks no translation is required.

I _think_ the efficient way to solve this is to detangle the hashing code from the encoding translation code (right now it is tangled in the hashing of characters). Instead, the hashing should assume that any translation has already occurred. 

We should call `obj_translate_encoding()` from either inside `init_dict_impl()`, or in each of the functions that use the dictionary, like `vec_unique()`, `vec_count()`, etc. While the latter feels repetitive, I think it is the more efficient option. `vec_match()` and `vec_in()` create dictionaries with `init_dict()` and `init_dict_partial()`, but they have already pre-translated their inputs using `obj_translate_encoding2()`. So putting `obj_translate_encoding()` into `init_dict_impl()` would be repetitive for them. 

Removing the translation code from the hashing code would solve another similar repetitive problem that currently occurs with `vec_match()`/`vec_in()`. Currently, they pre-translate their input, but then build the dictionary, which calls `hash_fill()`. Inside there, each character vector is currently checked _again_ to see if it needs translation.

This is all a bit brain melting, but I think this solution would work nicely as a long term fix.

title: Encoding test failures on Windows
description:
There are a number of failures related to string encodings on Windows that don't occur on Mac/Linux. These aren't errors in the underlying code, but the tests don't take into account the fact that `Encoding(x) <- "unknown"` does different things on Windows than it does on Mac/Linux.

For example:

Mac:

``` r
utf8 <- "\u00B0C"
utf8
#> [1] "°C"

unknown <- utf8
Encoding(unknown) <- "unknown"
unknown
#> [1] "°C"

utf8 == unknown
#> [1] TRUE

vctrs::vec_equal(utf8, unknown)
#> [1] TRUE
```

Windows:

``` r
utf8 <- "\u00B0C"
utf8
#> [1] "°C"

unknown <- utf8
Encoding(unknown) <- "unknown"
unknown
#> [1] "Â°C"

utf8 == unknown
#> [1] FALSE

vctrs::vec_equal(utf8, unknown)
#> [1] FALSE
```

So, we are doing the same as base R, but a few tests expect the result to be `TRUE` because I didn't have access to a Windows computer to test against at the time. 

I think the right thing to do is just check the result against base R when the results should be the same (I do this already).

When we purposefully diverge from base R (iterating row wise on data frames), we can either skip on windows or have an `if(on_windows())` branch in the test

title: `vec_equal_na(NA_real_)` returns a logical that internally is -1
description:
On a Windows Server 2019 build running 64-bit R, we get the following, where the `-1` should be a `1`:

```r
> .Internal(inspect((vec_equal_na(NA_real_))))
@0x00000241f470bbb0 10 LGLSXP g0c1 [] (len=1, tl=0) -1
```

This causes these tests to fail:

https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/da5db68f88cab710facc3603f1f6fddac84b2570/tests/testthat/test-equal.R#L176

https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/da5db68f88cab710facc3603f1f6fddac84b2570/tests/testthat/test-equal.R#L177

The problem is that `isnan()`, which is used [here](https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/da5db68f88cab710facc3603f1f6fddac84b2570/src/equal.c#L457) for checking if a double is an NA value, does _not_ consistently return 1 or 0, but instead just returns a non-zero integer or 0. The fix is to use base R's `ISNAN()`, which is a thin wrapper around `isnan()` defined as `isnan(x) != 0`.

I assume this means we will take a small performance hit because we have an extra comparison check, and a conversion from boolean to integer, but the conversion cost is probably quite low.

We also use `isnan()` [in a few other places](https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/search?utf8=%E2%9C%93&q=isnan&type=), but never as the return value. We use it in an `if () {}` condition, which should be safe, so I will leave those as is.

(I will submit a PR)

title: vec_unique() is sensitive to the marked encoding, where base::unique() is not
description:
*See below for a more minimal reprex.*

<details>
<summary>Long backstory</summary>
The troublesome object comes from https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/issues/722. It presents as a problem with `tidyr::unnest()` but I've narrowed it down to a very weird phenomenon with `vctrs::vec_rbind()`. I've pulled out the relevant list-column here, as just a list of tibbles.

``` r
result_ok <- list(
  tibble::tibble(
    `Max Temp Flag` = character(0),
    `Min Temp (°C)` = character(0),
    `Min Temp Flag` = character(0),
    `Mean Temp (°C)` = character(0)
  ),
  tibble::tibble(
    `Max Temp Flag` = rep(NA_character_, 6),
    `Min Temp (°C)` = rep(NA_character_, 6),
    `Min Temp Flag` = rep(NA_character_, 6),
    `Mean Temp (°C)` = rep(NA_character_, 6)
  )
)

bad_df_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
curl::curl_download(
  "https://gist.github.com/paleolimbot/ec9b62b758ae57a5b4669fa771fc40a0/raw/e96b55f54d68b1cb3877bb358b28b99dc8836ceb/bad_df.rds",
  bad_df_file
)
result_bad <- readRDS(bad_df_file)[["result"]]
```

The only apparent difference is in the attributes of the tibble components,
i.e. the presence of `flag_info`.

``` r
str(result_ok)
#> List of 2
#>  $ :Classes 'tbl_df', 'tbl' and 'data.frame':    0 obs. of  4 variables:
#>   ..$ Max Temp Flag : chr(0) 
#>   ..$ Min Temp (°C) : chr(0) 
#>   ..$ Min Temp Flag : chr(0) 
#>   ..$ Mean Temp (°C): chr(0) 
#>  $ :Classes 'tbl_df', 'tbl' and 'data.frame':    6 obs. of  4 variables:
#>   ..$ Max Temp Flag : chr [1:6] NA NA NA NA ...
#>   ..$ Min Temp (°C) : chr [1:6] NA NA NA NA ...
#>   ..$ Min Temp Flag : chr [1:6] NA NA NA NA ...
#>   ..$ Mean Temp (°C): chr [1:6] NA NA NA NA ...
str(result_bad)
#> List of 2
#>  $ :Classes 'tbl_df', 'tbl' and 'data.frame':    0 obs. of  4 variables:
#>   ..$ Max Temp Flag : chr(0) 
#>   ..$ Min Temp (°C) : chr(0) 
#>   ..$ Min Temp Flag : chr(0) 
#>   ..$ Mean Temp (°C): chr(0) 
#>   ..- attr(*, "flag_info")=Classes 'tbl_df', 'tbl' and 'data.frame': 0 obs. of  2 variables:
#>   .. ..$ flag       : chr(0) 
#>   .. ..$ description: chr(0) 
#>  $ :Classes 'tbl_df', 'tbl' and 'data.frame':    6 obs. of  4 variables:
#>   ..$ Max Temp Flag : chr [1:6] NA NA NA NA ...
#>   ..$ Min Temp (°C) : chr [1:6] NA NA NA NA ...
#>   ..$ Min Temp Flag : chr [1:6] NA NA NA NA ...
#>   ..$ Mean Temp (°C): chr [1:6] NA NA NA NA ...
#>   ..- attr(*, "flag_info")=Classes 'tbl_df', 'tbl' and 'data.frame': 13 obs. of  2 variables:
#>   .. ..$ flag       : chr [1:13] "A" "C" "E" "F" ...
#>   .. ..$ description: chr [1:13] "Accumulated" "Precipitation occurred, amount uncertain" "Estimated" "Accumulated and estimated" ...
```

In particular, the sub-tibble names appear to be the same.

``` r
nms_ok <- lapply(result_ok, names)
nms_bad <- lapply(result_bad, names)
identical(nms_ok, nms_bad)
#> [1] TRUE
identical(nms_ok[[1]], nms_ok[[2]])
#> [1] TRUE
identical(nms_bad[[1]], nms_bad[[2]])
#> [1] TRUE
```

But we get a different result from `vec_rbind()`. The columns with a special
character in the name aren’t correctly “matched up” with `result_bad` and we
get two copies.

``` r
vctrs::vec_rbind(!!!result_ok)   # 4 variables --> correct
#> # A tibble: 6 x 4
#>   `Max Temp Flag` `Min Temp (°C)` `Min Temp Flag` `Mean Temp (°C)`
#>   <chr>           <chr>           <chr>           <chr>           
#> 1 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> 2 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> 3 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> 4 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> 5 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> 6 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>
vctrs::vec_rbind(!!!result_bad)  # 6 variables --> wrong
#> # A tibble: 6 x 6
#>   `Max Temp Flag` `Min Temp (°C)` `Min Temp Flag` `Mean Temp (°C)`
#>   <chr>           <chr>           <chr>           <chr>           
#> 1 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> 2 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> 3 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> 4 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> 5 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> 6 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> # … with 2 more variables: `Min Temp (°C)` <chr>, `Mean Temp (°C)` <chr>
```

Stripping the `flag_info` attribute doesn’t rescue this. Seems irrelevant.

``` r
result_stripped <- result_bad
attr(result_stripped[[1]], "flag_info") <- NULL
attr(result_stripped[[2]], "flag_info") <- NULL
vctrs::vec_rbind(!!!result_stripped)
#> # A tibble: 6 x 6
#>   `Max Temp Flag` `Min Temp (°C)` `Min Temp Flag` `Mean Temp (°C)`
#>   <chr>           <chr>           <chr>           <chr>           
#> 1 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> 2 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> 3 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> 4 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> 5 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> 6 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> # … with 2 more variables: `Min Temp (°C)` <chr>, `Mean Temp (°C)` <chr>
```

The problem goes away with less challenging names, even without removing the
`flag_info` attribute.

``` r
result_renamed <- result_bad
names(result_renamed[[1]]) <- letters[1:4]
names(result_renamed[[2]]) <- letters[1:4]
vctrs::vec_rbind(!!!result_renamed)

#> 1 <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA> 
#> 2 <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA> 
#> 3 <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA> 
#> 4 <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA> 
#> 5 <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA> 
#> 6 <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>
```

Directly assigning the exact same names fixes it.

``` r
result_renamed_direct <- result_bad
nms <- c("Max Temp Flag", "Min Temp (°C)", "Min Temp Flag", "Mean Temp (°C)")
names(result_renamed_direct[[1]]) <- nms
names(result_renamed_direct[[2]]) <- nms
vctrs::vec_rbind(!!!result_renamed_direct)
#> # A tibble: 6 x 4
#>   `Max Temp Flag` `Min Temp (°C)` `Min Temp Flag` `Mean Temp (°C)`
#>   <chr>           <chr>           <chr>           <chr>           
#> 1 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> 2 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> 3 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> 4 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> 5 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> 6 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>
```

Re-assigning the same names this way does not fix it.

``` r
result_renamed_reassign <- result_bad
names(result_renamed_reassign[[1]]) <- names(result_bad[[1]])
names(result_renamed_reassign[[2]]) <- names(result_bad[[2]])
vctrs::vec_rbind(!!!result_renamed_reassign)
#> # A tibble: 6 x 6
#>   `Max Temp Flag` `Min Temp (°C)` `Min Temp Flag` `Mean Temp (°C)`
#>   <chr>           <chr>           <chr>           <chr>           
#> 1 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> 2 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> 3 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> 4 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> 5 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            
#> 6 <NA>            <NA>            <NA>            <NA>
```

``` r
result_renamed_indirect <- result_bad
nms <- names(result_bad[[1]])
names(result_renamed_indirect[[1]]) <- nms
names(result_renamed_indirect[[2]]) <- nms
```

title: Is vec_c() name repair with data frames correct?
description:
The third and fourth examples here are inconsistent, I think. I think outer names should probably be ignored for data frames here? `vec_rbind()` allows you to create a `.names_to` column, but I don't think we want that. The alternative is using outer names as row names but I don't think we want that either.

``` r
library(vctrs)

# (looks good) inner names used
vec_c(data.frame(xx = 1), data.frame(yy = 2))
#>   xx yy
#> 1  1 NA
#> 2 NA  2

# (looks good) row names ignored - i think this is on purpose?
vec_c(data.frame(xx = 1, row.names = "r1"), data.frame(yy = 2, row.names = "r2"))
#>   xx yy
#> 1  1 NA
#> 2 NA  2

# outer names used for columns?
# I think these should either have been used for row names (ew)
# or ignored? Then xx and yy would be the actual column names
vec_c(x = data.frame(xx = 1), y = data.frame(yy = 2))
#>    x  y
#> 1  1 NA
#> 2 NA  2

# I assume this error has something to do with how names are treated above
# It's trying to construct a column name vector of `c("x", "y")` but the resulting
# data frame should only have 1 column. Again, they should either become row
# names or get ignored
vec_c(x = data.frame(xx = 1), y = data.frame(xx = 2))
#> Error in vec_c(x = data.frame(xx = 1), y = data.frame(xx = 2)): 'names' attribute [2] must be the same length as the vector [1]
```

title: Implement simplified `new_list_of()` constructor in C
description:
To construct `list_of<>` objects from C, it would be useful to have a simplified constructor there. 

This would also have performance benefits for lists/data frames since right now `new_list_of()` called from R goes through `new_vctr()` and `vec_set_attributes()`, which calls `attributes(x) <- attrib` resulting in 2 copies of the list. This can be painful if the list is very large.

See this comment/issue for more information on how it should be implemented:
https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/pull/515#issuecomment-516841230

Also replace this ad hoc section with the constructor when implemented:
https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/59783eebbd885b4f0474a7352b07f6b77f8c1509/src/dictionary.c#L435

I'm imagining: `new_list_of(SEXP x, SEXP ptype)` that checks that `x` is a list and that `ptype` has size `0`, calls `r_maybe_duplicate(x)`, then runs the two `setAttrib()` lines already used in the section above

title: export vec_duplicate_split()
description:
For e.g. https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/pull/4504

`vec_duplicate_split()` gives exactly what is needed for a `vctrs` based implementation of `group_by()` , e.g. 

``` r
library(dplyr)

d <- tibble(x = c(1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2), y = c(1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2), z = 1:6)

vctrs:::vec_duplicate_split(select(d, x, y))
#> $key
#> [1] 1 2 5 6
#> 
#> $idx
#> $idx[[1]]
#> [1] 1 3
#> 
#> $idx[[2]]
#> [1] 2 4
#> 
#> $idx[[3]]
#> [1] 5
#> 
#> $idx[[4]]
#> [1] 6

group_by(d, x, y) %>% 
  group_data()
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#>       x     y .rows    
#> * <dbl> <dbl> <list>   
#> 1     1     1 <int [2]>
#> 2     1     2 <int [2]>
#> 3     2     1 <int [1]>
#> 4     2     2 <int [1]>
```

- `key` gives the indices I can use to `vec_slice()` the data to get the first columns
- `idx` is exactly the `.rows` column

https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/pull/4504 then goes a bit further to reveal empty groups when `.drop = FALSE` but that does not need to be `vctrs`' concern.

title: Massive speedup when `vec_slice()`ing using `[` (factors/dates)
description:
I'll try and do a PR for this tomorrow. I think performance here can be greatly improved by not constructing the call with the objects directly, but instead by using symbols.

https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/c9fb8834fc8b586b1ed0215667fe8c57e5e33f11/src/slice.c#L253

So something like:

```
      SEXP call = PROTECT_N(Rf_lang3(fns_bracket, syms_x, syms_i), &nprot);
      SEXP env = PROTECT_N(r_new_environment(R_GlobalEnv, 2), &nprot);
      Rf_defineVar(syms_i, index, env);
      Rf_defineVar(syms_x, x, env);
      out = PROTECT_N(Rf_eval(call, env), &nprot);
```

This gives us:

``` r
library(vctrs)

x <- factor(rep(letters, 10000))

# before
bench::mark(vec_slice(x, 1L))
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   expression            min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>       <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 vec_slice(x, 1L)   96.2µs    227µs     3651.    1.01MB     74.0

# after
bench::mark(vec_slice(x, 1L))
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   expression            min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>       <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 vec_slice(x, 1L)   9.42µs   10.8µs    89540.    17.1KB     89.6
```

title: vec_order() with a data frame column, not enough spicing
description:
``` r
library(vctrs)
library(tibble)

df <- tibble(x = 1:5, d = tibble(y = 1:5, z = 1:5, a = letters[1:5]))
vec_order(df)
#> Must use a vector in `[`, not an object of class matrix.
```

it's happening at the `exec` line in `order_proxy()` 

```r
    args <- unname(proxy)
    exec("order", !!!args, decreasing = decreasing, na.last = na.last)
```

because it's "not spliced enough" : 

``` r
library(vctrs)
library(tibble)

df <- tibble(x = 1:5, d = tibble(y = 1:5, z = 1:5, a = letters[1:5]))
proxy <- vec_proxy_compare(df)
  
order(proxy[[1]], proxy[[2]])
#> Must use a vector in `[`, not an object of class matrix.

# further spliced
order(proxy[[1]], proxy[[2]][[1]], proxy[[2]][[2]], proxy[[2]][[3]])
#> [1] 1 2 3 4 5
```

title: r_vec_fill(..., n) writes n+1 entries.  Causes vector overrun in names_to_col in vec_rbind()
description:
I noticed that in the following example vctrs-0.2.0's vec_rbind() writes one entry past the end of the names_to column that it constructs.
    df <- data.frame(X=11, Y=21)
    df4 <- vctrs::vec_rbind(A=df, B=df, C=df, D=df, .names_to="Names")
You can indirectly see this by adding R_PrintValue(names_to_col) after bind.c::vec_rbind's call to r_vec_fill.

This happens because r_vec_fill(,value,, n) writes n+1, not n, copies of value to the vector.  This is because of the +1 in the FILL macro.
```
    #define FILL(CTYPE, PTR, VAL_PTR, VAL_I, N)             \
      do {                                                  \
        CTYPE* data = (CTYPE*) PTR;                         \
        CTYPE* end = data + N + 1;                          \
        CTYPE value = ((const CTYPE*) VAL_PTR)[VAL_I];      \
                                                            \
        while (data != end) {                               \
          *data++ = value;                                  \
        }                                                   \
```
If I remove the +1 (so end is data+N) then it no longer writes off the end of the names_to array and all the testthat tests pass.  Is it possible that the n+1 behavior intentional?  If so, then vec_rbind() needs to call it with size-1 instead of with size.

title: vec_cbind returns wrong ptype
description:
Before `vec_cbind` is implemented by C,
`vec_cbind(grouped_df, data.frame)` returned `tbl_df`.

However, from b7f4518, it is returning `data.frame` and causing `tdiyr:::nest.grouped_df` also returning `data.frame`.

This change is causing messy printing of nested data frame because of using `print.data.frame` instead of `print.tbl` (https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/issues/675).

## vctrs 0.2.0

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(vctrs)
packageVersion("vctrs")
#> [1] '0.2.0'
d1 <- tibble(x=1:3)
d2 <- data.frame(y = 1:3)
vec_cbind(d1, d2) %>% class
#> [1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"
vec_cbind(group_by(d1, x), d2) %>% class
#> [1] "data.frame"
```

<sup>Created on 2019-07-05 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
```

title: 0-length recycling with `shape_broadcast()`
description:
This issue was originally mentioned in Slack.

Currently, you can `shape_broadcast()` from having 1 column down to having 0 columns. I am unsure if we want this behavior.

```r
library(vctrs)
#> Registered S3 method overwritten by 'vctrs':
#>   method                   from 
#>   as.character.rlang_error rlang

x <- matrix(1)
x
#>      [,1]
#> [1,]    1

y <- matrix(numeric(), nrow = 1, ncol = 0)
y
#>     
#> [1,]

# we lose the columns?
# we went "down" in dimension
vctrs:::shape_broadcast(x, y)
#>     
#> [1,]

# vec slice can "recycle" down to 0 rows
vctrs::vec_slice(x, 0)
#>      [,1]
```

title: Calling `colnames()` on a 1D array with `dimnames = list(NULL)` breaks
description:
The latest changes to `r_as_data_frame()` cause:

``` r
x <- array(c(1, 1, 2, 2, 3), dimnames = list(NULL))
vctrs::vec_unique_loc(x)
#> Error in dn[[2L]]: subscript out of bounds
```

Following this back, the culprit is `r_as_data_frame()` calling `vec_unique_colnames()` here
https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/ee9185941ea9b8d337c44df0eb14aee85fdb506e/src/utils.c#L782

Which calls base R's `colnames()` here
https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/a8393eba66094e13d916e5bdd741ff0440ff0269/src/names.c#L374

Apparently these are different:

``` r
y <- array(c(1, 1, 2, 2, 3))
colnames(y)
#> NULL

x <- array(c(1, 1, 2, 2, 3), dimnames = list(NULL))
colnames(x)
#> Error in dn[[2L]]: subscript out of bounds
```

Maybe `vec_unique_colnames()` should immediately return `NULL` if `has_dim(x) && vec_dim_n(x) == 1` so we don't call `colnames()`?

Or our C `colnames()` could check this, that would probably be more general in case we use `colnames()` in other places.

title: Subassignment with NA
description:
Subassignment with `NA` throws the error `No common type for x <logical> and value <vctr_class>` with a vector class built on `new_vctr()`. This is different from the CRAN version, and subassignment with `NA` works with a class built on `new_rcrd()`. Below is an example using the percent class from the S3 vignette.

```R
library(vctrs)

new_percent <- function(x = double()) {
  vec_assert(x, double())
  new_vctr(x, class = "vctrs_percent")
}

percent <- function(x = double()) {
  x <- vec_cast(x, double())
  new_percent(x)
}

format.vctrs_percent <- function(x, ...) {
  out <- formatC(signif(vec_data(x) * 100, 3))
  out[is.na(x)] <- NA
  out[!is.na(x)] <- paste0(out[!is.na(x)], "%")
  out
}

# Coercion
vec_type2.vctrs_percent <- function(x, y, ...) UseMethod("vec_type2.vctrs_percent", y)
vec_type2.vctrs_percent.default <- function(x, y, ..., x_arg = "", y_arg = "") {
  stop_incompatible_type(x, y, x_arg = x_arg, y_arg = y_arg)
}
vec_type2.vctrs_percent.vctrs_unspecified <- function(x, y, ...) x

# Casting
vec_cast.vctrs_percent <- function(x, to) UseMethod("vec_cast.vctrs_percent")
vec_cast.vctrs_percent.default <- function(x, to) vec_default_cast(x, to)

# with percent
vec_type2.vctrs_percent.vctrs_percent <- function(x, y, ..., x_arg = "", y_arg = "") x
vec_cast.vctrs_percent.vctrs_percent <- function(x, to) x

x <- percent(c(0.5, 1, 2))

# works
x[[1]] <- percent(0.75)
x[[1]] <- vec_na(percent())
vec_cast(NA, percent())

# Does not work
x[[1]] <- NA
```` 

If you do the same assignment with the `vctrs_rational` class from the S3 vignette the assignment works.

title: Feature request: obj_print_size() for displaying dimensions
description:
The recent change in `obj_print_header()` where `length()` is replaced by `vec_size()` makes it impossible to customise the dimension for the purpose of displaying.

``` r
library(vctrs)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

my_new_rle <- function(x = list(lengths = integer(), values = integer())) {
  new_vctr(x, class = "my_rle")
}

my_rle <- function(x) {
  my_new_rle(rle(x))
}
```

Previously,  defining `length()` provides a way for displaying the size.

```r
length.my_rle <- function(x) { # previously used for size display
  length(x$values)
}
```

Now, I need to define `obj_print_header()` to get the size properly displayed.

```r
obj_print_header.my_rle <- function(x) {
  cat(paste0(vec_ptype_full(x), "<", length(x), ">"))
  invisible(x)
}

x <- c(rep(1, 3), rep(3, 2), rep(10, 10))
my_rle(x)
#> my_rle<3> lengths   values 
#> 3, 2, 10 1, 3, 10
```

However, `vctrs_list_of` currently displays `vec_size()` instead of `length()`. This is not that informative for this `my_rle` class, because it's always a list of two elements. It would be more informative to show the number of runs. I understand `vec_size()` is more robust. Is it possible to provide `obj_print_size()` method for the displaying purpose?

```r
tbl <- tibble(x = rep(x, times = 3), group = rep(letters[1:3], each = 15))

tbl %>% 
  group_by(group) %>% 
  summarise(x_rle = list_of(my_rle(x)))
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>   group          x_rle
#>   <chr> <list<my_rle>>
#> 1 a                [2]
#> 2 b                [2]
#> 3 c                [2]
```

title: Question: vec_math not working if vec_proxy is defined
description:
This is more of a question, because my understanding about `vec_proxy` may not be correct.

I've defined a new class `my_rle`, a named list.

``` r
library(vctrs)
my_new_rle <- function(x = list(lengths = integer(), values = integer())) {
```

I'd like `sum()` over the `lengths` of `my_rle`. This works fine until I've defined `vec_proxy`.

I'd also like subsetting `my_rle` like a vector which goes beyond the list length 2. In this case, I need to define `vec_proxy`.

```R
legacy_repair <- function(nms, prefix = "V", sep = "") {
  if (length(nms) == 0) return(character())
  blank <- nms == ""
  nms[!blank] <- make.unique(nms[!blank], sep = sep)

  nms[blank] <- new_nms[seq_len(sum(blank))]
```

title: `vec_cast()` should use the nice `vec_type2()` error messaging
description:
I've been working on letting `hardhat` use `vctrs` for the checking of `new_data` you get at prediction time against the reference data used at fit time. The actual type casting implementation all seems correct, but the error messages are currently a bit frustrating to an end user. There are 3 main types of casting issues a user might see:

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(vctrs)
  library(gapminder)
  library(rlang)
})

options(rlang__backtrace_on_error = "none")

gap_train <- gapminder[1:3,]
gap_test <- gapminder[4:6,]

# 0 row reference slice
gap_train_0 <- vec_slice(gap_train, 0L)


# Case 1)
# Lossy cast warnings - too many columns

gap_test2 <- gap_test
gap_test2$x <- 1

vec_cast(gap_test2, gap_train_0)
#> Warning: Lossy cast from <tbl_df<
#>   country  : factor<bf6dc>
#>   continent: factor<69262>
#>   year     : integer
#>   lifeExp  : double
#>   pop      : integer
#>   gdpPercap: double
#>   x        : double
#> >> to <tbl_df<
#>   country  : factor<bf6dc>
#>   continent: factor<69262>
#>   year     : integer
#>   lifeExp  : double
#>   pop      : integer
#>   gdpPercap: double
#> >>.
#> Locations: 
#> Dropped variables: `x`
#> # A tibble: 3 x 6
#>   country     continent  year lifeExp      pop gdpPercap
#>   <fct>       <fct>     <int>   <dbl>    <int>     <dbl>
#> 1 Afghanistan Asia       1967    34.0 11537966      836.
#> 2 Afghanistan Asia       1972    36.1 13079460      740.
#> 3 Afghanistan Asia       1977    38.4 14880372      786.


# Case 2)
# Lossy cast warnings - at the individual column level

gap_test3 <- gap_test
gap_test3$country <- as.character(gap_test3$country)
gap_test3$country[1] <- "jupyter"

vec_cast(gap_test3, gap_train_0)
#> Warning: Lossy cast from <character> to <factor<bf6dc>>.
#> Locations: 1
#> # A tibble: 3 x 6
#>   country     continent  year lifeExp      pop gdpPercap
#>   <fct>       <fct>     <int>   <dbl>    <int>     <dbl>
#> 1 <NA>        Asia       1967    34.0 11537966      836.
#> 2 Afghanistan Asia       1972    36.1 13079460      740.
#> 3 Afghanistan Asia       1977    38.4 14880372      786.


# Case 3)
# Incompatible cast error - at the individual column level

gap_test4 <- gap_test
gap_test4$country <- as.numeric(gap_test4$country)

vec_cast(gap_test4, gap_train_0)
#> Error: Can't cast <double> to <factor<bf6dc>>
```

The issue here is that the error messages don't have enough information about where the problem came from (i.e. what column, what type of lossy cast it is).

For cases 2 and 3, one thing I have been playing with is the idea of catching and rethrowing warning / errors from inside `df_col_cast()`. This allows you to catch a lossy cast warning and add extra information about what column it came from, or even a more specific warning class. It's ugly, but the basic idea is:

```r
col_cast <- function(x, to, col) {
  rlang::with_handlers(
    vec_cast(x, to),

    vctrs_error_incompatible_cast = function(c) {
      c$message <- paste0(c$message, " ('", col, "')")
      c$col <- col
      class(c) <- c("vctrs_error_incompatible_column_cast", class(c))
      rlang::cnd_signal(c)
    },

    warning_lossy_cast = calling(function(c) {
      new_cnd <- c
      new_cnd$col <- col
      new_cnd$message <- paste0(new_cnd$message, " ('", col, "')")
      class(new_cnd) <- c("warning_lossy_column_cast", class(new_cnd))
      # must signal and muffle in this order?
      rlang::cnd_signal(new_cnd)
      rlang::cnd_muffle(c)
    })
  )
}
```

Then at [this line](https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/36dd5592c2bca27e426d84c8e043b43323cf9163/R/type-data-frame.R#L161) use `col_cast()` rather than `vec_cast()`:

```r
out[common] <- pmap(list(out[common], to[common], common), col_cast)
```

All that aside, you now get:

``` r
# Case 2)
# Lossy cast warnings - at the individual column level

vec_cast(gap_test3, gap_train_0)
#> Warning: Lossy cast from <character> to <factor<bf6dc>>.
#> Locations: 1 ('country')
#> # A tibble: 3 x 6
#>   country     continent  year lifeExp      pop gdpPercap
#>   <fct>       <fct>     <int>   <dbl>    <int>     <dbl>
#> 1 <NA>        Asia       1967    34.0 11537966      836.
#> 2 Afghanistan Asia       1972    36.1 13079460      740.
#> 3 Afghanistan Asia       1977    38.4 14880372      786.

catch_cnd(vec_cast(gap_test3, gap_train_0))$col
#> [1] "country"

class(catch_cnd(vec_cast(gap_test3, gap_train_0)))
#> [1] "warning_lossy_column_cast" "warning_lossy_cast"       
#> [3] "warning"                   "condition"


# Case 3)
# Incompatible cast error - at the individual column level

vec_cast(gap_test4, gap_train_0)
#> Error: Can't cast <double> to <factor<bf6dc>> ('country')

catch_cnd(vec_cast(gap_test4, gap_train_0))$col
#> [1] "country"

class(catch_cnd(vec_cast(gap_test4, gap_train_0)))
#> [1] "vctrs_error_incompatible_column_cast"
#> [2] "vctrs_error_incompatible_cast"       
#> [3] "vctrs_error_incompatible"            
#> [4] "rlang_error"                         
#> [5] "error"                               
#> [6] "condition"
```

I think some standard `cnd_modify()` type interface would be nice for something like this. Or maybe there is another way to pass this information along.

One other subtle nice thing here is that I would be able to tell that `warning_lossy_column_cast` would be different from a (not shown) `warning_lossy_dropped_variable_cast` later down the line.

title: `vec_compare(<type>, NULL)` throws an error
description:
Should this error?

``` r
vctrs::vec_compare(1:5, NULL)
#> Error: `x` and `y` must have same types and lengths
```

I think `integer(0)` might be an appropriate result, since that is what this does:

``` r
vctrs::vec_compare(NULL, NULL)
#> integer(0)
```

This error means that comparison operations between vctrs and `NULL` error, unlike base R, which I think gives an intuitive result:

``` r
vctrs:::new_hidden(1) > NULL
#> Error: `x` and `y` must have same types and lengths

1 > NULL
#> logical(0)
```

If it returned `integer(0)`, then the comparison operator would work since this operation powers `>.vctrs_vctr`:

``` r
integer(0) > 0
#> logical(0)
```

However, returning `integer(0)` would break an invariant of `vec_size_common(x, y) == vec_size(vec_compare(x, y))` so maybe it should be an error after all.

The current error is here at the C level. Since `vec_compare()` calls `vec_recycle_common()` and `vec_cast_common()` before this, I don't see how this error could ever be reached except in this 1 case with `NULL`. Maybe it could be improved some if that was the case?
https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/master/src/compare.c#L125

description:
@hadley depending on what is decided here, this might be a tidyr bug.

Modified from this tidyr issue:

What should this return? It seems natural here that `unchop()` should be using `vec_size()` (through `vec_is_empty()`) as it currently is (mapping over a list, checking the size of each element).

``` r
library(tidyr)
```

title: Some classes still need `vec_proxy_equal()`
description:
A change I noticed from `vec_proxy_equal()` in CRAN version to current implementation with `vec_proxy()` is that `vec_proxy_compare()` methods such as `sort()`, `max()` return the values from `vec_proxy(x)` and not `x`. The CRAN version returns the values of `x`, which seems to me to be preferable.

This makes it difficult to which value is equal to which index in x. It also causes unexpected differences in other places such as subsetting.

You can see an example of this in the S3 vignette with the Rational class. I think that the below provides the minimum to show this.

Thanks

```R
library(vctrs)

new_rational <- function(n = integer(), d = integer()) {
  vec_assert(n, ptype = integer())
  vec_assert(d, ptype = integer())
  
  new_rcrd(list(n = n, d = d), class = "vctrs_rational")
}

rational <- function(n, d) {
  c(n, d) %<-% vec_cast_common(n, d, .to = integer())
  c(n, d) %<-% vec_recycle_common(n, d)
  
  new_rational(n, d)
}

format.vctrs_rational <- function(x, ...) {
  # Access fields
  n <- field(x, "n")
  d <- field(x, "d")
  
  out <- paste0(n, "/", d)
  # Dealing with NA: Underlying data still present
  out[is.na(n) | is.na(d)] <- NA
  
  out
}

gcd <- function(x, y) {
  r <- x %% y
  ifelse(r, gcd(y, r), y)
}

vec_proxy.vctrs_rational <- function(x) {
  n <- field(x, "n")
  d <- field(x, "d")
  gcd <- gcd(n, d)
  
  data.frame(n = n / gcd, d = d / gcd)
}

vec_proxy_compare.vctrs_rational <- function(x) {
  field(x, "n") / field(x, "d")
}

# Changed slightly from S3 vignette to more clearly show issue
x <- rational(c(1, 2, 1, 2, 6), c(1, 1, 2, 2, 2))

# Sort works but shows values from vec_proxy(x) instead of from x
sort(x)

# Subsetting applies vec_proxy, and so though answers are equal, they are not the same
max(x)
max(x[-3])

# Compare
identical(max(x), max(x))
identical(max(x), max(x[-3]))
```

title: `vec_order()` on array inputs
description:
For array-like inputs with >2D, the following breaks the invariant of:

```
vec_size(vec_order(x)) == vec_size(x)
```

This happens because `order_proxy()` calls `order()` on the proxy object (which is just the array), but `order()` flattens its input.

``` r
library(vctrs)

vec_order(data.frame(x = 1:3, y = 1:3))
#> [1] 1 2 3

vec_order(matrix(1:6, ncol = 2))
#> [1] 1 2 3 4 5 6

vec_order(array(1:8, c(2, 2, 2)))
#> [1] 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8
```

This affects a few other things as well, like `vctrs:::xtfrm.vctrs_vctr` and `vec_sort()`

title: Bug with `hash_scalar()` affecting `vec_unique()` with arrays
description:
https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/79adc0f63552a87705fd326599419671b83b94a1/src/hash.c#L44

`hash_scalar()` is currently only looking at the _first_ value in each row for matrices / arrays. So you get strange behavior where sometimes matrices are seen as equal, when they clearly are not.

``` r
library(vctrs)

x <- matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 4), c(2, 2))
y <- matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 5), c(2, 2))

# these should clearly be different!
vec_unique(list(x, y))
#> [[1]]
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    1    3
#> [2,]    2    4

# the problem is that `has_scalar()`
# doesn't look at the entire row, just the first value
# in the row. So these are seen as different:
x <- matrix(c(2, 2, 3, 4), c(2, 2))
y <- matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 4), c(2, 2))

vec_unique(list(x, y))
#> [[1]]
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    2    3
#> [2,]    2    4
#> 
#> [[2]]
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    1    3
#> [2,]    2    4
```

<sup>Created on 2019-05-09 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1.9000)</sup>

This also affects the rest of the `vec_unique_*()` family, and maybe the duplicate functions too.

Maybe it makes sense to `vec_slice()` the i-th row, and then iterate over it, `hash_combine()`-ing the values?

title: Performance) `new_vctr()` overhead
description:
Currently, with R < 3.6.0, `new_vctr()` makes 4 copies every time it is called. Since this should be a really cheap function, I was hoping we could do something about this. As is, it's really killing my rray performance.

There are two main issues, both stem from the fact that `attributes(x) <- list(...)` creates two copies when there are attributes to set. See my examples below:

``` r
x <- 1:50000 + 0L
garbarge <- capture.output(profmem::profmem(attributes(x) <- NULL))

# set to nothing (same as setting to NULL)
x <- 1:50000 + 0L
profmem::profmem(attributes(x) <- list())
#> Rprofmem memory profiling of:
#> attributes(x) <- list()
#> 
#> Memory allocations:
#>        what  bytes      calls
#> 1     alloc 200048 <internal>
#> total       200048

# set attributes. Agh! Two copies!
x <- 1:50000 + 0L
profmem::profmem(attributes(x) <- list(stuff = "hi"))
#> Rprofmem memory profiling of:
#> attributes(x) <- list(stuff = "hi")
#> 
#> Memory allocations:
#>        what  bytes      calls
#> 1     alloc 200048 <internal>
#> 2     alloc 200048 <internal>
#> total       400096

# Clever way to call it, which only copies once
x <- 1:50000 + 0L
profmem::profmem(x <- `attributes<-`(x, value = list(stuff = "hi")))
#> Rprofmem memory profiling of:
#> x <- `attributes<-`(x, value = list(stuff = "hi"))
#> 
#> Memory allocations:
#> Number of 'new page' entries not displayed: 1
#>        what  bytes      calls
#> 2     alloc 200048 <internal>
#> total       200048
```

Based on the above results, I have two suggestions.

1) `validate_attr()` should validate and return names, but not set them. It will simply pass them on to `structure()`, ~which always removes all attributes from `.Data` before adding new ones.~ (not true, see the Update below)

2) We should wrap `structure()` so we have a version that does the exact same thing, except it sets attributes using `attributes<-(.Data, value = c(attributes(.Data), attrib))` since that only makes 1 copy, as seen above. Maybe call it `vec_structure_shim()`.

To be as forward compatible as possible, I think it would make sense to create this `vec_structure_shim()` in `.onLoad()`. If the version is >= 3.6.0, we can just use base R's provided `structure()`, which has fixed the double copy issue, and with ALTREP often makes 0 copies until needed. Otherwise, we use our shim.

PS: For the interested, I believe this `attributes<-()` double copy behavior might have been some kind of bug that was just fixed. There was a time between 3.5.3 and 3.6.0 where this was what `structure()` did, which leads me to believe that even after they had ALTREP parts in place, it was still making a copy because of some compiler bug. 
https://github.com/wch/r-source/commit/8d332d420f83c4343cf2e1a5694faeffc9de599e#diff-7eda0a571a9f91eb3be4d1627b8d4c2aL37

Here is a before/after performance comparison:

``` r
x <- 1:500000 + 0L
dim = c(5000L, 100L)

bench::mark(
  new_vctr(x, dim = dim),
  new_vctr2(x, dim = dim)
)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 10
#>   expression   min     mean   median    max `itr/sec` mem_alloc  n_gc n_itr
#>   <chr>      <bch> <bch:tm> <bch:tm> <bch:>     <dbl> <bch:byt> <dbl> <int>
#> 1 new_vctr(… 706µs   1.77ms   1.11ms 5.56ms      565.    7.65MB    43   152
#> 2 new_vctr2… 135µs 484.16µs 279.96µs 1.22ms     2065.    1.96MB    39   801
#> # … with 1 more variable: total_time <bch:tm>
```

Update) `structure()` does not actually remove existing attributes from `.Data`, but maybe this is ok? Otherwise I don't see a way to add _only_ the attributes in `...` without either rewriting `structure()` or making a second copy with `attributes(x) <- NULL`

title: Reconsider vec_ptype_abbr() for factor and complex
description:
After switching to `vec_ptype_abbr()` in {pillar}, two downstream packages now fail their checks. This is mostly due to the change from `"fct"` to `"fctr"` and `"cpl"` to `"cplx"` .

`type_sum()` moved *away* from `"fctr"` and `"cplx"` just over a year ago: https://github.com/r-lib/pillar/pull/80, suggested in https://github.com/r-lib/pillar/issues/71. It feels inconsistent that now `vec_ptype_abbr()` returns `"fctr"` and `"cplx"` .

@lionel- @hadley: Can we please move to `"fct"` and `"cpl"` here to save quite a few headaches downstream?

Thanks to @nacnudus for pointing this out: https://github.com/nacnudus/unpivotr/issues/24#issuecomment-490627895.

title: Is `[.vctrs_vctr` too restrictive for objects with shape?
description:
If you create a new vctr class that acts like a matrix and try and subset it, you immediately hit problems with `[.vctrs_vctr` only allowing `i` through.

``` r
library(vctrs)

new_2d <- function(.data, dim) {
  vctrs::new_vctr(.data, dim = dim, class = "vctrs_2d")
}

x <- new_2d(c(1, 2), dim = c(2L, 1L))

# works
x[1]
#> <vctrs_2d[1]>
#>      [,1]
#> [1,] 1

# nope
x[, 1]
#> `...` is not empty.
#> These dots only exist for technical reasons and should be empty.

# nope
x[1, 1]
#> `...` is not empty.
#> These dots only exist for technical reasons and should be empty.


# What _should_ it return?
# should it just pass on to 
# the matrix method and drop dimensions?
# (i.e. we say that the underlying class
# controls whether dims are dropped or not)
y <- matrix(1:2)
y[, 1]
#> [1] 1 2

# or should it return this?
y[, 1, drop = FALSE]
#>      [,1]
#> [1,]    1
#> [2,]    2

# same question here I guess
y[1, 1]
#> [1] 1
```

If you do pass everything on to the underlying class, I think it might be good to think through what these return:

```r
x[1] # might call `vec_slice_native()` and drop dims
x[1,] # might call underlying method and not drop dims
```

On a similar note, `[<-.vctrs_vctr` should allow more than just `i` through as well. But I don't think the fix is as simple as just replacing `i` with `...` there.

title: `vec_unique()` breaks with 2D+ arrays
description:
I believe this will be solved by #245 when the `dim` is retained by `vec_data()`, but felt it would be worth reporting now.

The issue is that `vec_data()` flattens matrices, which results in incorrect unique locations that are used to `vec_slice()` with.

``` r
library(vctrs)

x <- matrix(1:6, ncol = 2)

x
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    1    4
#> [2,]    2    5
#> [3,]    3    6

vec_unique(x)
#> Error: Can't index beyond the end of a vector.
#> The vector has length 3 and you've tried to subset element 4.

# should be c(1, 2, 3)
# currently it tries to `vec_slice()`
# with this
vec_unique_loc(x)
#> [1] 1 2 3 4 5 6

# the problem is an eventual call to 
# `vec_data()` through the chain:
# `vec_unique_loc()` -> `vec_proxy_equal()` -> `vec_proxy_compare()` -> `vec_data()`
vec_data(x)
#> [1] 1 2 3 4 5 6

# if we can give the C function the 
# right object, it does the right thing already
.Call(vctrs:::vctrs_unique_loc, x)
#> [1] 1 2 3
```

title: vec_restore.default() alters size and type
description:
According to the docs:

> A `vec_restore()` method can assume that `x` has the correct type (although the length may be different) but all attributes have been lost and need to be restored.

This would lead me to believe that `x` can have a different size than `to`, which is the case when using `vec_restore()` with 1D vectors, but with matrices/arrays this isn't the case because all attributes of `to` are copied to `x`, including the `dim` (which embeds the size).

``` r
library(vctrs)

x <- matrix(1:5)

# dummy function to demonstrate losing attributes
# - type is the same (but attributes are needed)
# - size is now different
c_level_manip <- function(x) {
  vec_data(x)[1:2]
}

# I think this should work
vec_restore(c_level_manip(x), x)
#> Error in attributes(x) <- attributes(to): dims [product 5] do not match the length of object [2]

# special case the `dim` attribute
# pull size from x
# pull shape from to
vec_restore.default <- function(x, to) {
  restore_attr <- attributes(to)
  
  if ("dim" %in% names(restore_attr)) {
    restore_attr$dim <- c(vec_size(x), vctrs:::shape(to))
  }
  
  attributes(x) <- restore_attr
  x
}

vec_restore(vec_data(x)[1:2], x)
#>      [,1]
#> [1,]    1
#> [2,]    2
```

<sup>Created on 2019-01-07 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1.9000)</sup>

Size is implicitly ignored with vectors:

``` r
library(vctrs)

ex <- factor(c("a", "a", "b"))

vec_restore(vec_data(ex[1]), ex)
#> [1] a
#> Levels: a b
```

<sup>Created on 2019-01-07 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1.9000)</sup>

Update) This also would affect dimnames and general names. This is more difficult as the order or the rows would matter here when "restoring" names, but generally I think it isn't vctrs's job to restore names/dimnames so maybe they could just be removed.

``` r
library(vctrs)
x <- 1:5
names(x) <- letters[1:5]
vec_restore(vec_data(x[1:2]), x)
#> Error in attributes(x) <- attributes(to): 'names' attribute [5] must be the same length as the vector [2]
```

title: R 3.1 - double dispatch requires explicit exports in packages that build on vctrs
description:
I noticed that in `probably`, I was failing travis on R 3.1 every time.

I've created a small repo that demonstrates the problem:
https://github.com/DavisVaughan/testtravis

The issue is this:
- Use `@importFrom vctrs vec_cast`
- Create a function that calls `vec_cast(thing, integer())`
- This should call `vec_cast.integer`
- Then more double dispatch...

This works everywhere except on R 3.1 where I get the error:

```
Error in vec_cast.integer(1, integer()) : 
  could not find function "vec_cast.integer"
```

See travis:
https://travis-ci.org/DavisVaughan/testtravis/builds/439111560

The failure line:
https://travis-ci.org/DavisVaughan/testtravis/jobs/439111566#L1868

If I explicitly do `@importFrom vctrs vec_cast.integer`, things work fine again.

My guess is that something must have changed from R 3.1 -> 3.2 where in 3.1 if you are dispatching to something that is another generic, R wouldn't recognize that as being a method of the first generic which it should be able to dispatch to without needing the method to be exported.

title: Should `vec_equal()` compare names?
description:
This would make it different from `c(a = 1) == c(b = 1)`. This might reflect a design difference between vctrs and base R.

* In base R, `==` compares `[[` slices of atomic vectors, hence the names are excluded from the comparison.

* In vctrs, atomic types do not have exposed atoms. Only recursive types allow extraction of data. `vec_equal()` operates on data proxys and hence is not affected by attributes in general. But vector names are special vector data with ad hoc support.

See also https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/issues/141#issuecomment-469727710.

More importantly, what are the practical implications of comparing names in `vec_equal()`?

title: vec_rbind with packed and nested data frames
description:
Real world examples of packed and nested data

## No packed / nested data frames

```r
#store all pages in a list first
baseurl <- "https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/api/v2/search.json?order=revenue&sort_order=desc"
pages <- list()
for(i in 0:10){
  mydata <- jsonlite::fromJSON(paste0(baseurl, "&page=", i))
  message("Retrieving page ", i)
  pages[[i+1]] <- mydata$organizations
}

# both OK
alldata1 <- jsonlite::rbind_pages(pages)
alldata2 <- dplyr::bind_rows(pages)

# not OK
alldata3 <- do.call(vctrs::vec_rbind, pages)
```


## Packed data frames

```r
# with packed data frames
urls <- sprintf('https://api.github.com/repos/tidyverse/ggplot2/commits?page=%d', 1:5)
pages <- lapply(urls, jsonlite::fromJSON)

# ok
alldata1 <- jsonlite::rbind_pages(pages)

# unsupported
alldata2 <- dplyr::bind_rows(pages)

# error
alldata3 <- do.call(vctrs::vec_rbind, pages)
```


## Nested data frames

The `flatten` argument in `fromJSON` converts packed into nested data frames:

```r


# with nested data frames
urls <- sprintf('https://api.github.com/repos/tidyverse/ggplot2/commits?page=%d', 1:5)
pages <- lapply(urls, jsonlite::fromJSON, flatten = TRUE)

# ok
alldata1 <- jsonlite::rbind_pages(pages)
alldata2 <- dplyr::bind_rows(pages)

#error
alldata3 <- do.call(vctrs::vec_rbind, pages)

```

title: Operators on base object types
description:
I understand method dispatch for the `Ops` generic as follows:

- If any of the objects involved is S4, try S4 method dispatch ([code](https://github.com/wch/r-source/blob/f421a17bd4fb559674a760667c088bdc5aa8093c/src/main/eval.c#L3578-L3591))
- Retrieve the method responsible for handling the operator both for the LHS and the RHS
    - If both methods are identical, continue ([code](https://github.com/wch/r-source/blob/f421a17bd4fb559674a760667c088bdc5aa8093c/src/main/eval.c#L3638))
    - If only LHS or RHS has a method, use this ([code](https://github.com/wch/r-source/blob/f421a17bd4fb559674a760667c088bdc5aa8093c/src/main/eval.c#L3658-L3664))
    - In a few hard-coded special cases (e.g. `Date + difftime`, `POSIXt + difftime`), use the LHS or RHS method without a warning ([code](https://github.com/wch/r-source/blob/f421a17bd4fb559674a760667c088bdc5aa8093c/src/main/eval.c#L3640-L3649))
    - Otherwise, give an "Incompatible methods" warning ([code](https://github.com/wch/r-source/blob/f421a17bd4fb559674a760667c088bdc5aa8093c/src/main/eval.c#L3651-L3652)) and **do not dispatch** (instead the operation is performed on bare values)

This is a problem for _hms_, which overrides the `"difftime"` class (see also https://github.com/tidyverse/hms/issues/18). There seems to be no way we can support `+.hms` (and by extension `+.vctrs_vctr`) without this "Incompatible methods" warning right now. Moreover, using operators on any vctrs subtype with a base object (date, time, difftime, factor) will inevitably lead to this warning, and also to a possibly wrong implementation (as in the case of `Date + hms`).

Possible options include:

- Hijack `+.difftime` and other operators, e.g. both `+.difftime` and `+.POSIXt` must point to the same implementation
    - Pretty sure CRAN won't be happy about this
- Implement an S4 class that can serve as a base for other classes that need it
- Don't support operators for base object types, provide regular functions like `vec_add()` et al. that dispatch to `vec_arith()`
- We could suggest that base R makes this warning optional, e.g. if the S3 method has a specific attribute
    - base R still recommends to use S4, not sure how likely this is

title: Base R coercion methods should use shape_broadcast()
description:
Currently, this is being used:

```r
as.double.vctrs_vctr <- function(x, ...) {
  vec_cast(x, double())
}
```

But if I have a class that extends `vctrs_vctr` and it a matrix-ish class, then this will fail:

```r
as.double(my_vctrs_mtrx_obj)
```

It fails because the `to` shape is too strict. It should adapt to `x`. You could just do:

```r
as.double.vctrs_vctr <- function(x, ...) {
  vec_cast(x, shape_broadcast(double(), x))
}
```

This would probably be implemented for `double`, `integer`, `logical` and `character`.

My use case is in extending `vctrs_vctr` with an array class on top of it, `vctrs_rray`. I need to be able to do:

title: Should vec_type2.factor.factor return sorted levels?
description:
Right now, this behavior occurs which is somewhat consistent with the hacky way you can combine factors in base R.

``` r
library(vctrs)

fct1 <- factor(c("a", "b"))
fct2 <- factor(c("b", "c"))

vec_type2(fct1, fct2)
#> factor(0)
#> Levels: a b c
vec_type2(fct2, fct1)
#> factor(0)
#> Levels: b c a

# base R behavior
# this is the only way to combine them?
unlist(list(fct1, fct2))
#> [1] a b b c
#> Levels: a b c
unlist(list(fct2, fct1))
#> [1] b c a b
#> Levels: b c a

# this doesnt work
c(fct1, fct2)
#> [1] 1 2 1 2
```

But with `vec_type2()`, you are creating a "new" common type from the underlying types. One could argue that the new type could follow the same procedure that a factor takes when being created from a character vector, sorting levels alphabetically:

```r
# a "fresh" factor has sorted levels
factor(c("b", "a"))
#> [1] b a
#> Levels: a b
```

This would make `vec_type2(fct1, fct2) = vec_type2(fct2, fct1)` in this example. It would require `levels_union()` to sort the levels.

I'm not particularly tied to either implementation, but @topepo mentioned that he thinks it might be more consistent with base R to sort them

title: converting Date into POSIXct when time zone is not UTC
description:
We now see:
```r
library(vctrs)
Sys.setenv(TZ = "EST") # anything non-UTC
vec_c(Sys.Date(), Sys.time())
# [1] "2018-10-03 00:00:00 EST" "2018-10-03 13:47:22 EST"
c(as.POSIXct(Sys.Date()), Sys.time())
# [1] "2018-10-02 19:00:00 EST" "2018-10-03 13:47:22 EST"
```
which means that unlike base R, `vctrs` conversion of `Date` to `POSIXct` depends on your time zone settings. I think this is not a good idea: R scripts would become non-reproducible across time zones.

What we want is that the way times are printed depends on time zone, not the values we assign during conversion. Also, deviating here from base R is asking for trouble.

title: Complete lubridate support

```R
new_Period <- function() lubridate::seconds(integer())
new_Duration <- function() lubridate::dseconds(integer())

vec_type2.Interval.default <- function(x, y) stop_incompatible_type(x, y)

vec_type2.Duration.Period   <- function(x, y) new_Period()

vec_type2.Period.Interval   <- function(x, y) new_Period()

vec_type2.Duration.Duration <- function(x, y) new_Duration()

vec_type2.Duration.Interval <- function(x, y) new_Duration()
vec_type2.Interval.Duration <- function(x, y) new_Duration()

# vec_type2.difftime.difftime <- function(x, y) new_Duration()

vec_type2.Interval.difftime <- function(x, y) new_difftime()

# vec_cast ----------------------------------------------------------------

vec_cast.Period <- function(x, to) UseMethod("vec_cast.Period")
vec_cast.Duration <- function(x, to) UseMethod("vec_cast.Duration")
vec_cast.Interval <- function(x, to) UseMethod("vec_cast.Interval")

vec_cast.Duration.default <- function(x, to) stop_incompatible_cast(x, to)
vec_cast.Interval.default <- function(x, to) stop_incompatible_cast(x, to)

vec_cast.Period.Period     <- function(x, to) x

vec_cast.Period.difftime   <- function(x, to) lubridate::as.period(x)
```

title: Recycling data frames
description:
Should these recycle the data frame to length zero?

```r
shape <- vec_shape(integer())
vec_reshape(mtcars, shape)
#> Error: Can only recycle data frame along rows

shape <- vec_shape(matrix(nrow = 0, ncol = 1))
vec_reshape(mtcars, shape)
#> Error: Can only recycle data frame along rows

shape <- vec_shape(matrix(nrow = 0, ncol = 0))
vec_reshape(mtcars, shape)
#> Error: Can only recycle data frame along rows
```

Same for recycling 1-row dataframes to length n:

```r
shape <- vec_shape(integer(3))
vec_reshape(mtcars[1, ], shape)
#> Error: Can only recycle data frame along rows
```

Currently the dimensions have to match completely:

```r
shape <- vec_shape(matrix(nrow = 0, ncol = ncol(mtcars)))
vec_reshape(mtcars, shape)
#>  [1] mpg  cyl  disp hp   drat wt   qsec vs   am   gear carb
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)

shape <- vec_shape(matrix(nrow = 3, ncol = ncol(mtcars)))
vec_reshape(mtcars[1, ], shape)
#>   mpg cyl disp  hp drat   wt  qsec vs am gear carb
#> 1  21   6  160 110  3.9 2.62 16.46  0  1    4    4
#> 2  21   6  160 110  3.9 2.62 16.46  0  1    4    4
#> 3  21   6  160 110  3.9 2.62 16.46  0  1    4    4
```

Maybe that's because I need directional recycling instead of full shape recycling?

Maybe the errors could be a little more informative to help figure out why the recycling can't be done.

title: Some notes
description:
Since [comments are welcome](https://twitter.com/hadleywickham/status/1026204037765627904), some thoughts.

I think that having a list type that forces all objects to be of the same class can be really useful. I do have questions about introducing a new set of atomic types.

R has a type system that can already be confusing, there is 

- `typeof`, determining the R internal type
- `mode` is a type designation that's closer to user experience (see below)
- `storage mode` giving something closer to physical storage type (e.g. `double` for a value of type `numeric`)
- `class`  and `inherits` for basic types and (`S3`, `S4`, `RC`,...) class extensions and best for users.

Some examples
```r
> types <- function(x) c(class=class(x)
  , typeof=typeof(x), mode=mode(x), storage.mode=storage.mode(x))
> dat <- list(int=1L,real=pi, complex=2+3i, string = character(), cat=factor(), binary=as.raw(0), fun=function(){})

> dat <- list(integer=1L,real=pi, complex=2+3i
  , string = character(), categorical=factor(), binary=as.raw(0)
  , 'function'=function(){})
> t(sapply(dat, types))
            class       typeof      mode        storage.mode
integer     "integer"   "integer"   "numeric"   "integer"   
real        "numeric"   "double"    "numeric"   "double"    
complex     "complex"   "complex"   "complex"   "complex"   
string      "character" "character" "character" "character" 
categorical "factor"    "integer"   "numeric"   "integer"   
binary      "raw"       "raw"       "raw"       "raw"       
function    "function"  "closure"   "function"  "function"  
```

So the question is if another `atomic' type designation just for the benefit of stricter coercion rules will help users. In my experience, it is already uncomfortable having to explain novice users the difference between data frames and tibbles. This is necessary because they will run into both very quickly once they start doing actual work with R. When you are a new user, this is another thing to put on your mental stack that has nothing to do with _getting things done_. This is even more true for vector types. For example, until now, I can explain R's coercion rules fairly easily, by letting people experiment with a few lines of code like:

```r
c(10, "hello")
```
Then, when I ask them to explain what happened and why, this usually clears things up pretty quickly.

With these new vector types new users would have to grok a second type system, especially if you automatically translate everything that is (implicitly) translated to a tibble. [By the way, beyond R's usual behavior, I think that type casts should be asked for by the user explicitly (_Explicit is better than implicit_)].

So in conclusion, I do not feel that the benefits of stricter coercion rules outweigh the burden of having to cope with an extra system for atomic types for end-users. I see there may be benefits for (package) developers. So it should be developer-facing rather than user-facing.

title: argument name antipattern
description:
Having special names for some arguments when the other arguments are absorbed into everything else is an antipattern because the function can't tell between the argument as a special argument or as an unspecial named argument. Example:
```
vec_c(1, 2, .type = integer())
#> [1] 1 2
```

`vec_c` supports named vectors, so `vec_c(a=1, b=2, .type=integer())` is valid, but `vec_c(.print=1, .type=2, .screen=3)` fails because the `.type` argument is treated specially.

The arguments for this antipattern are:

- The low probability of having an argument with that name is very low  - but that probability is non-zero and increases linearly with the amount of usage. When it hits it generates massive surprise.
- Names starting with a dot are well-known as "special" and are documented - but this relies on people being introduced to the documentation at first usage.

The existence of specially-named arguments when there is a possibility of misinterpretation is an irregularity which seems incongruous with everything else being tidy.

You could write `vec_c` to return a function, and then pass the type argument as a further argument:

```
vec_c(a=1, .type=99, type=23)()  # returns c(a=1,.type=99, type=23)
vec_c(a=1, .type=99, type=23)(type=integer()) # as above but integer type.
```

This approach has the advantage that the argument no-longer needs to be "dotted".

title: Coercion rules
description:
Rules:
- integer + double -> double
- logical NA + anything -> anything
- factor + factor (same levels) -> factor
- factor + factor (diff levels) -> character (WARN)
- factor + character -> character (WARN)
- dates + datetime -> date time
- datetime + datetime (different tz) -> date time (first tz)

Implement in C, and provide replacement to `dplyr::combine()`

``` R
# Integer coerced to double
df <- data_frame(x = 1:2) %>%
  group_by(x) %>%
  summarise(y = if (x == 1) 1L else 1)
expect_type(df$y, "double")

df <- data_frame(x = 1:2) %>%
  group_by(x) %>%
  mutate(y = if (x == 1) 1L else 1)
expect_type(df$y, "double")

df1 <- data_frame(x = 1L)
df2 <- data_frame(x = 1)
df <- bind_rows(df1, df2)
expect_type(df$x, "double")
expect_type(combine(df1$x, df2$x), "double")

df <- inner_join(df1, df2, by = "x")
expect_type(df$x, "double")
```
